title: Data is everywhere (you make it right now)
real_life: while you read this, your phone logs GPS pings, heart rate, battery drain and which app you opened. That stream of facts is data — it exists whether or not anyone looks at it.
intuition: Every tap, step and swipe writes a record. A data analyst turns raw records into answers and decisions.

what_moves.description: Data is just facts stored as text and numbers: "Ana", 42, "2026-09-18 14:03". The analyst's job: ask the right question, pull the records that answer it, and check the answer is believable.

key_points: A record (row) describes one thing — one customer, one order, one sensor ping.
A field (column) is one kind of fact about that thing — name, amount, timestamp.
Big questions ("why did revenue dip?") are answered from tiny facts.
If it can't be measured and written down, a computer can't count it.

quiz.q: A heart-rate watch saves one reading every 30 seconds for a full day. How many records is that?
options: about 2,880
1 record
a field, not data
too few to count as data
quiz.why: 1 day = 86,400 seconds ÷ 30 = 2,880 separate readings. Each reading is one record in the heart_rate field.

title: What a data analyst actually does
real_life: a doctor doesn't guess your illness. She asks what you feel (question), takes vitals (collect), rules out the routine (clean/check), runs the tests that matter (analyze), shows you the result (visualize), and only then prescribes (decide).
intuition: A fixed pipeline, every single time: question → data → clean → analyze → show → decide.

what_moves.description: Every analytics project — a $10 dashboard or a billion-dollar fraud model — walks this same line. Watch it below. Nothing in this course ever leaves this pipeline; each later phase is one station of it, zoomed in.

key_points: The question decides everything else — a sharp question saves weeks of work.
Cleaning is usually 50–80% of the effort; plan for it, don't pretend.
The deliverable is a decision, not a chart. Charts are the argument.
If any station lies, the decision lies — that's why every step is checkable.
labels: press ▶ Play — the packet walks all six stations

quiz.q: Your manager says "customers are leaving, find out why". The FIRST station you work on is…
options: writing the precise question
buying more data
picking the fanciest chart
training a model
quiz.why: "Customers leaving" could mean churn, refunds, or one bad week. Until the question is measurable ("churn rate rose 12% in tier-2 in June"), every later step is guesswork.

title: How to use this course (60-second version)
real_life: learning to drive. You don't memorize the engine diagram first — you watch the instructor, then sit in the car and feel each gear, one at a time, until it's muscle memory.
intuition: Every step follows the same rhythm: read one idea, play the motion, touch the controls, answer one question.

what_moves.description: This course has

key_points: Green box = real-life version of the idea. Read it first — it's the anchor.
Play / ▶ buttons = the motion. Always press them once; the animation is the explanation.
Sliders & clicks on the canvas = your turn. Break things on purpose.
Answer the question, read the why, then press Next. One step = one idea, nothing more.
labels: four moves, one idea at a time

quiz.q: A step's question was answered wrong and you see the explanation. What happens to your progress?
options: the step is done once you understand it — answer again to mark it
the step is failed, you can never pass it
progress is lost entirely
nothing; wrong answers are not recorded
quiz.why: Wrong answers are private and unlimited — the course is a practice ground, not an exam hall. Mark it done by answering correctly once; the 'why' is shown for every answer so you learn from both.

title: Tables: rows are things, columns are facts
real_life: your phone's Contacts app. One row per person. Columns: Name, Number, City. You rarely care about the storage — you tap a name and it's there. SQL is how you ask for exactly the rows you want.
intuition: Almost every system on Earth — banks, Netflix, hospitals — stores data in tables: named columns of facts, one row per thing.

what_moves.description: Each row is a record; each column a field with one type (text, number, date). Click column headers below to sort, and click any cell to pin it. Types matter: a price of "19.99" (text) can't be summed by the machine — it will silently skip it.

key_points: Row = record: one customer, one order, one ping.
Column = field: one kind of fact, one type (text / number / date).
Duplicate rows are allowed unless you say otherwise (unique constraint).
Every serious database can be read this way — SQL is the shared language on top.
labels: click a header to sort · click a cell to pin it

quiz.q: The column signup_date stores "2026-07-04". Why is the date format (not a number) the safer choice?
options: dates must stay text so sorting & math stay correct across time zones and calendars
numbers are slower
text takes less space
databases can't store dates
quiz.why: Dates carry meaning (ordering, differences, time zones). Stored as text they sort wrong ("2026-9-1" vs "2026-10-01"), and arithmetic like "days since signup" becomes hand-work. Databases have a real DATE type for exactly this.

title: WHERE — keep only the rows you asked for
real_life: a 40-person group chat. You don't read all 3,000 messages — you filter: "from Ana, contains 'meeting', this week." That's WHERE from='Ana' AND body LIKE '%meeting%' AND day >= '2026-09-11'.
intuition: A table answers "everything". A question is almost always about a subset — WHERE is how you name that subset.

what_moves.description: WHERE compares each row and keeps the ones that pass. Combine conditions with AND (both must pass), OR (one is enough), NOT (invert). Toggle conditions below and watch rows disappear.

key_points: WHERE runs row by row: pass → keep, fail → drop.
AND is stricter (smaller result); OR is looser (bigger result).
IS NULL tests for missing — = NULL would never work (missing ≠ equal to anything).
Big tables: WHERE is also where performance lives — the engine can skip most rows if you write it well (see indexes).

quiz.q: Which query returns customers who live in Lyon AND spent more than 30?
options: WHERE city='Lyon' AND amount>30
WHERE city='Lyon' OR amount>30
WHERE city='Lyon' OR amount>30 AND city='Lyon'
WHERE city LIKE 'Lyon' > 30
quiz.why: AND means both tests must pass on the same row. The OR version also returns big spenders from other cities — a different, wider question. Option 3 actually equals A, but A is the honest way to write it.

title: GROUP BY + aggregates — from rows to answers
real_life: splitting a restaurant bill four ways. You don't argue over each of the 14 items — you group them by table and each table pays its subtotal. Buckets first, then one number per bucket.
intuition: "How much did each city spend?" — GROUP BY piles rows into buckets; aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT) give each bucket one number.

what_moves.description: Rule that trips everyone: every column you show must either be grouped or aggregated. If you ask "name, city, SUM(amount)" — which Ana? The engine refuses, and it's right. Click a city bucket to see its rows fold in.

key_points: GROUP BY city → one row per city; the rest must go through SUM/AVG/COUNT/MIN/MAX.
HAVING filters after grouping ("cities with SUM > 100"); WHERE filters rows before.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips missing values — often a data-quality tell.
This one pattern (bucket → summarize) is 80% of business reporting.
labels: SELECT city, COUNT(*) n, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY city
click a bar (or bucket) to fold its rows in

quiz.q: Why must every non-grouped column in the SELECT pass through an aggregate?
options: otherwise the result row would contain multiple possible values — ambiguous
aggregates are faster
databases forbid extra columns
GROUP BY already aggregates everything automatically
quiz.why: If you group by city but show name, the city bucket contains 3 different names. The engine can't pick one without lying. Either group by it too, or aggregate it (e.g. COUNT(name)).

title: JOINs — combining two tables on a shared key
real_life: a party guest list (names) and a seat map (table numbers). To invite each person to their table, you match by name: Ana → table 3. People without a seat? That's a LEFT JOIN decision, not an accident.
intuition: A name lives in one table, the address in another. JOINs stitch rows together where a key matches — the single most-used operation in analytics.

what_moves.description: Both tables must share a key (here id). Pick a join type below and watch which row pairs survive. NULL (red) means "no match found, but keep me anyway."

key_points: INNER: only pairs that match — the default, the safest.
LEFT: keep every left row; unmatched ones get NULLs (great for finding orphans).
RIGHT/FULL: mirror images — keep the other side too. FULL keeps everything on both sides.
CROSS: every row × every row (n×m) — a deliberate explosion, rarely wanted.
labels: keys: people.id = cities.id · unmatched rows keep NULL (red)

quiz.q: You need "all customers, and their order count if any — but keep customers who never ordered". Which join?
options: LEFT JOIN orders ON customer_id
INNER JOIN orders
FULL JOIN orders
CROSS JOIN orders
quiz.why: LEFT keeps every customer row; customers with no matching order still appear, with NULL (count → 0 after COALESCE). INNER would silently drop them — the classic lost-customer bug.

title: CTEs & subqueries — answer in stages
real_life: a school science fair. Stage 1: each class votes for its best project. Stage 2: the judges compare the class winners — not all 120 projects. The class-winner list is your CTE: a named intermediate table.
intuition: Hard questions are two easy ones. A CTE (WITH x AS (…)) names the first answer, then the second question builds on it.

what_moves.description: Watch the two stages below. Stage 1 computes "top spender per city"; stage 2 asks a question about those winners only. Without the CTE you'd repeat the whole stage-1 computation inside stage 2 — or worse, get it subtly different.

key_points: WITH winners AS (…) = "pretend this table exists"; use it by name afterwards.
CTEs can reference earlier CTEs — a chain of named stages.
Subqueries do the same inside a SELECT/WHERE; CTEs are usually more readable.
Each stage is independently checkable — that's the debugging superpower.
labels: WITH winners AS ( SELECT city, MAX(amount) m FROM orders GROUP BY city )
stage 1 done — its result is now a named table
stage 2 answered the real question — 2 cities

quiz.q: A CTE is best described as…
options: a named, temporary result you can query like a table
a faster version of JOIN
a way to store data permanently
an index on a column
quiz.why: It exists only for that one statement, but inside it you use it exactly like a real table. It does not speed things up by itself — it makes multi-stage logic readable and testable.

title: Window functions — rank & running totals without collapsing
real_life: a running race with age categories. The scoreboard shows every runner (not just one per category) — each with "1st in 30–39" and the total time of everyone ahead. Two facts per row, rows never lost.
intuition: GROUP BY crushes rows into one per bucket. Window functions do the math alongside the rows — each row keeps its identity, plus a computed badge.

what_moves.description: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat ORDER BY time) ranks within each category. SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY t) gives a running total. Click a category below to spotlight its ranking.

key_points: PARTITION BY = buckets that never merge rows (unlike GROUP BY).
ORDER BY inside OVER() decides the ranking / running order.
row_number (unique), rank (gaps on ties), dense_rank (no gaps) — pick by tie policy.
Running totals + RANK = the tool behind 90% of "leaderboard" dashboards.
labels: name  cat  time  ·  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY cat ORDER BY time)
rows keep their identity — rank & total are attached, never collapsed

quiz.q: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) on scores 90, 90, 80 gives ranks…
options: error — ties are forbidden
quiz.why: Both 90s take rank 1; the next rank jumps to 3 (a gap). dense_rank would give 1,1,2; row_number would force 1,2,3 arbitrarily. Ties are everywhere in real data — the policy is a feature, not a bug.

title: Indexes & B-trees — why "WHERE id=42" is instant
real_life: finding a word in a 1,200-page book. Without the index: read from page 1. With the index: "gradient — see p. 812", two lookups. Your phone's contacts do this for every name you type.
intuition: A table with no index is a stack of papers — every search reads everything. An index is a layered signpost: a few hops, then done.

what_moves.description: A B-tree keeps keys sorted on each level; each hop narrows the search to ~1/n of the rest. Press ▶ to search for 42 and watch the hop count (right) stay at 3 while the linear scan (below) crawls row by row.

key_points: Linear scan = O(n): 10M rows → up to 10M comparisons.
B-tree search = O(log n): 10M rows → ~24 comparisons, same every time.
Indexes cost space and slow down INSERT/UPDATE (they must be kept in sync).
One index per queried column is not the answer — the optimizer picks; over-indexing backfires.
labels: searching for key 42 in a B-tree index
no index: check row 1, row 2, row 3 … until 42 shows up
press ▶ — each hop discards ~90% of the remaining keys
hop 1: key 42 lives in the 40–49 decade — 9 of 10 branches discarded
hop 2: unit 42 found. The whole search took 3 levels — the linear scan just read 42 rows and is still going

quiz.q: A table has 1,000,000 rows. With a B-tree index on the searched column, a single-key lookup needs roughly…
options: 20–25 hops
1,000 hops
1 hop
quiz.why: log2(1,000,000) ≈ 20; real B-trees fan out far wider than 2 (100–1000+ children per node), so it's often fewer hops. That logarithmic flatness — 10 rows or 10 billion rows — is the whole magic of the index.

title: Transactions & ACID — the bank transfer promise
real_life: a money transfer. Either both accounts update or neither does — there is no "half-sent." ACID is the contract that makes that true even when the power fails mid-transfer.
intuition: "Move €50 from Ana to Ben" is two writes. If the machine dies between them, money is created or destroyed. A transaction makes that impossible.

what_moves.description: Play the transfer. On step 3 the bank "crashes" (toggle it on before playing) — watch ROLLBACK restore both balances, or COMMIT bank the change. Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable — four words, one promise.

key_points: Atomic: all-or-nothing — the unit of all-or-nothing is the transaction.
Consistent: every rule (total money is constant) holds before and after.
Isolated: two transfers at once don't see each other's half-states.
Durable: after COMMIT, even a crash can't take the money back.
labels: ROLLED BACK — both balances restored. Total money never changed.
COMMITTED — durable: even a power cut now cannot undo it.
credited. The COMMIT makes it permanent

quiz.q: Mid-transaction, after Ana's debit but before Ben's credit, the server loses power. On restart, the balances are…
options: both unchanged — the whole transaction rolled back
Ana debited, Ben not — the partial write survived
both debited
unknown — depends on timing
quiz.why: Atomic + durable WAL: the uncommitted debit was never made permanent, so recovery reverts it. The invariant (total = same) can never be broken, even at the worst possible moment.

title: Normalization — don't store the same fact twice
real_life: a family recipe book where " Grandma's oven runs 20° hot" is scribbled under every recipe. She fixes the oven — which recipe notes stay wrong? Normalization: write the oven note once, on the oven's page.
intuition: If the department manager's name sits in 200 employee rows, one promotion means 200 edits — and the 199 you forget are now lies.

what_moves.description: Left: one table where dept_manager repeats on every employee row (3rd normal form violation). Click the manager's name — every dependent row that must be edited at once lights up. Right: the manager moves to its own table; employees keep a tiny dept_id foreign key.

key_points: 1NF: one value per cell, no repeating groups.
2NF: no partial dependence (a fact about the dept must not live in a row keyed by employee+dept).
3NF: no transitive dependence — dept → manager is a dept fact, store it with the dept.
Foreign keys (dept_id) are the glue: small, typed, unambiguous.
labels: click "Mira" — every dependent cell that a promotion must touch
employees point at D1 — never repeat the name

quiz.q: In the denormalized table, the manager gets promoted. How many cells must change?
options: one row per employee in that department
just one, in the header
zero — managers aren't stored
the whole table
quiz.why: The manager's name is repeated in every employee row of the department. Change one and the rows disagree (inconsistency). Normalized: one cell in the dept table changes; every employee sees the new name automatically.

title: Mean, median, mode — three centers, three stories
real_life: an office where 10 people earn €35–65k and the CEO earns €500k. "Average salary €89k" (mean) describes nobody. "Typical salary €48k" (median) describes a real person. The mean was pulled up by one outlier.
intuition: "Average" hides three different ideas. Which one you use changes the story — sometimes on purpose.

what_moves.description: Mean = everything pooled and split evenly (sensitive to extremes). Median = the middle row (robust). Mode = the most common value. Add the CEO below and watch the two lines diverge.

key_points: Mean is a balance point — outliers drag it.
Median is a crowd middle — add any number of outliers, it barely moves.
Mode is the typical case — best for categories (most popular size, color).
Reporting "the average" without saying which is how numbers lie politely.
labels: the CEO dragged the mean up

quiz.q: Salaries: [35, 38, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52, 55, 60, 65, 500] (k€). Which statement is true?
options: mean ≈ 89, median = 48 — the outlier pulled the mean
mean ≈ 48, median ≈ 89
mean and median both ≈ 500
the median changed more than the mean
quiz.why: Sum = 980 → mean ≈ 89.1. Sorted, the 6th of 11 values is 48 → median. Ten values barely moved; the mean jumped. That's why "typical salary" should almost always be a median.

title: Spread: standard deviation — how wild is the data?
real_life: choosing a restaurant. "Average rating 4.0" means nothing if one week is 1.9 and the next 6.1. You'd rather know the range you can expect: 4.0 ± 0.2 or 4.0 ± 1.8?
intuition: Two waiters average the same tips (€15). One is boringly reliable; the other is a slot machine. The average can't tell them apart — spread can.

what_moves.description: Standard deviation (σ) = "typical distance from the average." The ±1σ band holds ~68% of normal data. Slide the variability and watch the same average look completely different.

key_points: σ answers "how surprised should I be?" — small σ = predictable.
Variance = σ² — same information, squared (used inside formulas).
For normal data: ~68% of values within mean±1σ, ~95% within mean±2σ.
IQR (middle 50%) is the robust cousin when outliers distort σ.
labels: waiter tips (€) — same average, different σ

quiz.q: Same average, two datasets: σ=0.5 and σ=5. Which is true?
options: σ=5 is far less predictable — values scatter 10× wider
σ=5 has more data
they are equally predictable
σ=0.5 is the wilder one
quiz.why: σ is literally the typical distance from the mean. 5 vs 0.5 is a 10× difference in surprise — the average alone was telling you nothing about it.

title: Distribution shape — click to build it yourself
real_life: adult heights are bell-shaped (most people average, few extremes). Incomes are right-skewed (many modest, a few enormous). Same tools read both — you just learn to name the shape.
intuition: A distribution is just a crowd of numbers, sorted into a skyline. Its shape (center, spread, tails) is the story.

what_moves.description: Click the canvas to add random values (blue = first worker, pink = second). Load the income preset and flip the "normal overlay" to see the fit. Watch the mean (red) and median (green) as your shape changes.

key_points: Symmetric bell ≈ normal — mean = median, σ does the talking.
Right skew: mean > median (a long right tail drags the mean).
Left skew: mean < median.
Tails = risk: heavy tails mean "what usually happens" hides rare, huge events.
labels: distribution builder — click to add values
preset: bell-shaped — click canvas to add points, or flip presets

quiz.q: A dataset has mean 60, median 52, and a long tail to the right. Most likely it is…
options: right-skewed (a few very large values)
left-skewed
perfectly normal
uniform (all values equally likely)
quiz.why: Mean > median is the classic right-skew signature: the tail on the right drags the mean above the middle. Think incomes: a few millionaires pull the average above the typical person.

title: Correlation vs causation — the ice-cream trap
real_life: "umbrella sales correlate with sunburns". Nobody thinks umbrellas cause sunburn. Correlation = "these move together"; causation = "this one makes the other happen". Confusing the two is how companies waste budgets on fake levers.
intuition: Ice-cream sales and shark attacks rise and fall together, r ≈ 0.9. Eating ice cream does not summon sharks. A third thing — summer heat — drives both.

what_moves.description: Three presets below: a real link (study time → grades), a confounded link (ice cream ↔ sharks), and pure noise. Click the canvas to add your own points and watch r move. Strong r never proves cause — it only says "look, they're connected."

key_points: r ranges −1…+1: strength AND direction of a linear link.
r=0.9 says nothing about cause, direction, or a hidden third variable.
Classic confounders: season, population size, "more stores of X" = "more people buying X".
The escape hatches: controlled experiments (A/B tests) or carefully argued mechanisms.
labels: ice-cream sales ↔ shark attacks (confounded by summer)

same r as a 'real' link —
shape can't see the confounder

r measures the linear link
only. It never names a cause.
click canvas to add points · r updates live

quiz.q: Two datasets both have r = 0.95. A: study hours vs exam score. B: ice-cream sales vs shark attacks. What can we honestly conclude?
options: both show a strong linear link; only A plausibly has a direct causal mechanism
both are proven causation
B is a stronger link because it's stranger
neither is a real link
quiz.why: Correlation is the same number in both — it measures connection, not cause. A has a plausible mechanism (learning → better answers); B is almost certainly a summer-heat confound. Strong r is the start of a story, never its proof.

title: Sampling & the law of large numbers
real_life: opinion polls. Nobody asks all 10 million voters — a random sample of 1,000 is right within ±3 points. But 1,000 people who already voted online (not random) can be wrong by 20+ points.
intuition: You can't taste the whole ocean — you taste a spoonful. Sampling works when the sample is random, and the bigger the spoonful, the closer it gets to the truth.

what_moves.description: A fair coin: truth = 50% heads. Play flips and watch the running proportion wobble wildly at first, then settle. Slide the sample size and see how the 95% "confidence band" tightens around the truth.

key_points: Random = every unit has a chance — that's what makes the math honest.
Small samples wobble: with n=10, 8 heads (80%) is normal noise, not a biased coin.
Large samples settle: the band shrinks like 1/√n.
Non-random samples can be wrong at ANY size — the math only rescues randomness.
labels: flipping a fair coin — running share of heads

quiz.q: A poll of 1,000 random voters shows candidate A at 52% (±3). What is the honest read?
options: A is ahead by 2–5 points, or it's a coin flip — the margin of error overlaps 50%
A wins by exactly 2%
the poll is useless
A wins by 52 points
quiz.why: 52% ± 3 means the true support could be 49–55%. The 50% line sits inside the band, so "ahead" and "tied" are both compatible with the data. That's why elections inside the margin of error are called too close to call.

title: Probability: binomial & Poisson — counting rare events
real_life: binomial — a vending machine works 99% of the time; what's the chance 3 of your next 10 drinks fail? Poisson — support tickets arrive ~4/day; what's the chance tomorrow brings 8? (Rare things pile up when you wait long enough.)
intuition: Probability is just "how often would I see this if the world worked the way I think it does?" Two workhorses: binomial (fixed tries) and Poisson (rare arrivals).

what_moves.description: Left: binomial bars P(exactly k successes) with n tries and per-try probability p. Slide both. Right: Poisson for arrivals with average λ per window. These curves are how SREs size on-call and how insurers price risk.

key_points: Binomial: fixed n independent tries, each success prob p. The bars always sum to 1.
The binomial peak sits near n·p — "expected value = n × p".
Poisson: counts of rare, independent arrivals in a window; λ = average count.
"Rare × many chances" = surprisingly common: 1% failure × 1,000 requests ≈ 63% chance of ≥1 failure.
labels: binomial: fixed tries (coin, API calls) · Poisson: arrivals in time (tickets, calls, crashes)

quiz.q: A payment API fails 1% of calls. A user makes 100 calls. Chance of at least one failure is…
options: about 63%
about 1%
about 10%
essentially 0
quiz.why: P(no failure in 100) = 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.366, so P(≥1 failure) ≈ 63%. Single-event rates understate what happens in bulk — this is why 99%-reliable systems still need retries, and why "four nines" (99.99%) exists.

title: Confidence intervals & hypothesis testing — "is this real?"
real_life: a drug trial. The new pill beats the old by 4 mmHg — but with 50 patients that gap could be luck. The question is never "what did we measure?" but "if there were NO real effect, how often would data this extreme show up?" That frequency is the p-value.
intuition: Every measurement is truth + noise. A confidence interval is an honest shrug with bounds: "the effect is in this range, 95 times out of 100."

what_moves.description: Below: the truth slider sets reality (0 = the pill does nothing). Each ▶ run measures 30 patients and reports the observed effect, its 95% CI, and the verdict. Set truth to 0 and run 10 times — you'll watch ~5 "false alarms" happen purely by luck. That's the 5% error rate everyone agrees to accept.

key_points: 95% CI: build it 100 times, ~95 will cover the true value. (It's about the method, not one interval.)
p < 0.05: "if nothing were real, this result would happen < 5% of the time" → reject the null.
Small n → wide CI → everything is "maybe." Power comes from sample size.
A non-significant result ≠ proof of nothing; it means "not enough evidence".
labels: is the new pill real? (each ▶ = one trial of 30 patients)
(slider below — try 0 and run several times)
— the expected ~5% is the agreed cost, not a bug

quiz.q: A study finds effect = 2.1, 95% CI [−0.5, 4.7], p = 0.12. The honest conclusion:
options: the data are compatible with no effect — not enough evidence to claim one
the effect is exactly 2.1
the effect is zero
the study failed
quiz.why: The CI crosses 0 and p > 0.05: "no effect" is inside the plausible range. We can't claim the effect is real — but we also can't prove it's zero. "No evidence" and "evidence of none" are different statements.

title: A/B testing — the only clean causation machine
real_life: a shop testing two checkout buttons. 10,000 shoppers each, random split. Green: 4.2% complete purchase. Blue: 3.1%. Random assignment means the groups were (statistically) identical people — so the gap is the button's doing, not a coincidental crowd difference.
intuition: Correlation watches; experiment does. Split users randomly, change exactly one thing, and the difference in outcomes is the effect — confounders have no time to sneak in.

what_moves.description: Slide the true lift (what the new design really does) and the sample size, then play. Watch how tiny effects need huge n to become "significant" — and how a 0-lift still produces fake winners ~5% of the time.

key_points: Random split = the engine that kills confounders. Change ONE variable at a time.
Significant = the observed gap would be this big by luck alone < 5% of the time.
Power: small lift + small n → mostly "no verdict." Bigger n is the only honest fix.
Peeking daily and stopping at the first "significant" inflates false wins (the peeking problem).
labels: A/B test — control vs new design
recent trials (dot = observed lift, line = 95% band):

quiz.q: You A/B test a headline. With 200 users it's "significant" on day 1, but by day 5 it's not. Sound practice?
options: decide on a pre-set sample size (e.g. 5,000) before looking; the day-1 'win' was peeking
trust the day-1 win — significance doesn't un-happen
stop the test and ship — you have evidence
run it forever until it's significant again
quiz.why: With enough checks, chance alone will flash "significant" (~5% of any single check). Pre-committing the sample size means exactly one final judgment — that's what keeps the 5% error rate honest.

title: Variables, types & flow — the recipe of a program
real_life: a recipe says "heat 2 eggs". You don't re-heat the eggs every time the recipe mentions eggs — "eggs" is a label for the thing in your hand. Code works the same: the name is a pointer, not the value.
intuition: A program is a recipe the machine follows in order. A variable is a labelled jar: put a value in, read it out, overwrite it — the label always points at the newest value.

what_moves.description: Trace the four lines below. The watch box on the right shows every jar after each line. Note line 3: "sum: " + str(y) — a sentence made by gluing text and a number (Python won't glue them unless you convert).

key_points: Names point at values; x = 5 then x = 7 means x is 7 — the 5 is gone.
Types matter: 5 + "5" is an error in Python; "5" * 3 is "555".
str(), int(), float() convert between types — data work is 50% conversions.
Flow is top-to-bottom; if is the only place the recipe forks.

quiz.q: What does print("19.99" * 2) do?
options: prints "19.9919.99" — strings multiply by repeating
prints 39.98
prints "19.992"
raises an error
quiz.why: Python strings multiply by REPEATING: "19.99" * 2 = "19.9919.99". No error, but clearly not money math — the classic reason data columns must be numeric types before you do arithmetic.

title: Lists, dicts & sets — three ways to group things
real_life: your to-do list (order matters: shower before work). Your contacts (you look up by NAME, not by shelf position). The friends you've already messaged (you only care "have I?" — duplicates are meaningless).
intuition: A list is an ordered shelf (positions matter). A dict is a phonebook (key → value, order irrelevant). A set is a guest list with no repeats (membership only).

what_moves.description: Left: a list — click a position to insert 40, click the end to pop. Right: a dict — click a key to fetch its value in one hash. Notice the dict never cares about order; the list never cares about keys. Picking the wrong container is the most common beginner slowness.

key_points: List [..]: ordered, indexable, duplicates OK. append O(1); inserting at position 0 is O(n).
Dict {k: v}: key→value, lookup O(1) average (a hash table under the hood).
Set {..}: unique values, "in" check O(1) — the dedup tool of choice.
If you find yourself looping to look for something, you probably need a dict/set instead of a list.
labels: click a slot to insert 40 there · click past the end to pop
click a key — the dict finds it without scanning, O(1)

quiz.q: You need to count how many times each word appears in a sentence of a million words, fast. The right tool is…
options: a dict: word → count, update one key per word
a list: scan the whole list for each word
a set: it remembers words
nothing — you must sort the sentence
quiz.why: Dict lookup is O(1): one hash per word → total O(n). A list scan per word is O(n²) — a million words means a trillion operations. 'Count things' is the dict's signature move (collections.Counter does exactly this).

title: Loops & comprehensions — do it to every item
real_life: washing 12 dishes: you do the same 3 moves to each dish, one after another. for dish in pile: wash(dish) — the pile is data, wash is the function, the loop is the habit.
intuition: Data work is 90% "do this to each row." A loop is the machine's version of "take the next one from the pile." A comprehension is the same idea in one line — the idiom you'll see everywhere.

what_moves.description: Left: the classic for-loop, stepped tile by tile. Right: the same work as squares = [x*x for x in nums] — read it right-to-left: "for each x in nums, keep x*x." If you can say a comprehension out loud in English, you own it.

key_points: for x in coll: — Python hands you each item; avoid tracking indexes by hand.
Comprehension: [expr for x in coll if cond] = map + filter in one line.
range(n) gives 0…n−1 — the classic off-by-one source: it stops BEFORE n.
Loops transform item by item — the output list grows one item per pass.

quiz.q: [x*x for x in range(4)] produces…
options: an error
quiz.why: range(4) = 0,1,2,3 — it stops before 4. Squared: 0,1,4,9. The "stops before n" rule is the #1 off-by-one in Python; range(1,5) would give 1..4 → [1,4,9,16].

title: Functions — named machines with input, body, output
real_life: a coffee machine. You press "latte" (call with argument), the machine does 40 hidden steps (the body), and gives you a cup (the return value). You don't need to know the boiler pressure — that's what encapsulation is for.
intuition: A function is a vending machine: hand it an input (coin), it runs a fixed process, hands back an output. The caller never sees (or cares about) the mechanism.

what_moves.description: Step through square(4): the call creates a frame (a private workspace with its own x), the body computes, and return hands the value back to the caller. Two calls with different inputs reuse the same body — that's the whole point.

key_points: def name(params): defines once; name(args) calls any number of times.
Each call gets a FRESH frame — its variables don't leak out (local scope).
return ends the call and hands back exactly one value.
No return = None — a function that only prints or mutates returns nothing.
labels: /3 — a fresh frame per call, no shared state

quiz.q: def f(a): a = a + 1; return a — then x = 5; f(x); print(x) prints…
options: 5 — the function's change stayed in its frame
6 — the return updated x automatically
None
an error
quiz.why: The +1 happened to the frame's own variable, not to x. The return value went nowhere (not assigned), so x is untouched. To change x you'd write x = f(x) — functions hand values back; they don't reach into the caller's pockets.

title: pandas DataFrames — the spreadsheet that obeys
real_life: a spreadsheet, but instead of clicking filters you type the intent: "give me the rows where amount > 20, grouped by city, summed." One sentence = one pipeline, re-runnable on next month's data without re-clicking.
intuition: pandas is a table in memory with a brain: select columns, filter rows, group, fill gaps — each operation returns a new table you can chain. This is 80% of day-to-day analyst code.

what_moves.description: A dirty 6-row frame below (one missing amount, one duplicate, two small rows). Play the 4 cleaning steps and watch the frame shrink and transform. The chain df.dropna().drop_duplicates()… reads left-to-right like a sentence.

key_points: A DataFrame = columns of one type + an index. Think "typed table."
df[col] selects, df[cond] filters, df.groupby(col).agg() summarizes.
.dropna() / .fillna() / .drop_duplicates() are the three dirty-data basics.
Operations return NEW frames — the original is untouched until you assign (chain-friendly).
labels: steps: 1 drop NaN → 2 drop dups → 3 keep amount>20 → 4 group by city
press ▶ — four cleaning steps on the same frame
→ then one groupby sentence summarizes it all

quiz.q: df.groupby('city')['amount'].sum() returns…
options: one row per city with the summed amount
every original row with a sum column
a single total for the whole table
an error — you must filter first
quiz.why: groupby picks the bucket key ('city'), ['amount'] picks the column, .sum() picks the aggregate → one number per bucket: the canonical 'total per city' in one line.

title: NumPy & vectorization — one op on a million items
real_life: moving 1,000 bricks. Hand-carrying: 1,000 trips. Conveyor belt: press one button, the whole line moves. Same work — the second version doesn't do it 'faster per brick', it stops paying the driver's salary (interpreter overhead) per brick.
intuition: Python loops are slow because every step is a full interpreter round-trip. NumPy pushes the whole operation into optimized C running on the array at once — "vectorization" is why data science lives on NumPy/pandas.

what_moves.description: Race below: the left lane does for i: out[i] = xs[i] * 2 (one brick per tick). The right lane does xs * 2 (the whole belt at once). Both end with the same output; watch the counters.

key_points: import numpy as np; xs = np.array([…]) = a typed, contiguous array.
xs * 2 multiplies EVERY element — no loop visible, C code underneath.
Typical speedup 50–1000× on real-sized data; that's the entire pitch.
pandas is built on NumPy — df.col * 2 gets the same win on tables.
labels: same output — the vector lane finishes in one push while the loop lane pays per element

quiz.q: Why is xs * 2 (NumPy) much faster than a Python for-loop doubling each element?
options: the loop pays interpreter overhead per element; NumPy runs one optimized C pass over the array
NumPy uses more RAM so it's faster
the loop has a bug
identical speed — the marketing says otherwise
quiz.why: Each Python iteration is dispatch + type checks + a method call — microseconds wasted × a million. NumPy compiles the whole op into a tight C loop over contiguous memory. Same math, ~100× fewer 'driver salaries'.

title: EDA: load → clean → explore → visualize → question
real_life: a chef's mise en place. Before cooking: wash the vegetables, chop what's rotten away, lay everything out, taste a spoonful. You never cook from a dirty crate — and you never skip the tasting.
intuition: Exploratory Data Analysis is the fixed ritual before any modeling: get it in, fix what's broken, look at everything, then let the data ask you questions you didn't think to ask.

what_moves.description: Chips = records. Two are dirty (one missing value, one duplicate). Play the pipeline and watch the dirty chips get flagged at the cleaning station, and the visualize station turn the survivors into a chart. The last station is the payoff: a question the data raised.

key_points: EDA output is QUESTIONS, not answers — "why is Lyon's amount 3× Paris's?" is a great EDA result.
The 4 classics to check: missing values, duplicates, outliers, type mix-ups.
Plot EVERY numeric column (histograms) — the first pass catches 80% of the surprises.
EDA is iterative: each question sends you back for a second look.
labels: press ▶ — the EDA ritual, chip by chip
· the chart raised a question — EDA done

quiz.q: Your EDA shows a column 'age' with values [23, 45, 190, 31, 88]. The right EDA move is…
options: investigate where 190 comes from (data entry? different scale?) before anything else
silently drop it — one row can't matter
round it to 90 so it looks normal
change the column type to text
quiz.why: One weird value is a clue about the pipeline, not noise to sweep away. It might be a data-entry bug, a different unit, or a genuinely important edge case. EDA means 'go find out' — never 'assume and delete'.

title: What is ML? Learn the rule from examples, don't write it
real_life: you don't teach a child "what is a dog" with a 40-page definition. You point at 50 dogs. The child builds the rule internally — ML does the same with numbers instead of eyes.
intuition: Classic code: you write the rules, the computer follows them. ML: you show labeled examples, the machine finds a general rule that explains them — and applies it to things it has never seen.

what_moves.description: Same task two ways. Approach A (rules) works until every edge case needs its own line. Approach B (learning) keeps one model and improves it when it gets something wrong — that loop is all of machine learning.

key_points: A model is a function f(x) → prediction whose INSIDE gets tuned automatically, not hand-written.
Labels (the answers) are the teacher; unlabeled data is the raw material.
Generalization = performing well on NEW data — the only metric that counts.
Every ML project is the same loop: predict → measure error → adjust → repeat.
labels: Task: label new emails SPAM or HAM
A: rules work… until every edge case grows its own line
B: one model, tuned from the labeled examples — new email in, decision out

quiz.q: A rule-based spam filter misses a new trick ("URGENT!! you won"). You add another rule. Next month, 4 more tricks. This pattern shows…
options: rules don't scale — every new pattern needs human maintenance; a learned model absorbs new examples instead
the code is buggy
spam is a hard problem — nobody could solve it
you need a faster computer
quiz.why: Hand-written rules grow one line per exception, forever. A learned model re-fits on new labeled examples: same one artifact, updated — that's the core economic argument for ML.

title: Train / validation / test — never peek at the exam
real_life: a student who rehearses only the exact mock exam questions scores 98% in rehearsal and 40% on the real exam. Validation is the next mock; the test set is the real exam — taken ONCE.
intuition: A model graded on the data it studied from looks brilliant. Graded on data it never saw, reality speaks. The split exists to keep those two numbers honest and separate.

what_moves.description: 20 labeled rows below. Step through: the TRAIN stack teaches, the VALIDATION stack helps you tune choices (learning rate, depth), and the TEST stack is graded exactly once for the final report. If the test ever influences a decision, its number is worthless.

key_points: Typical split: ~70–80% train, ~10–15% validation, ~10–15% test — all random, all disjoint.
Tuning on the test = data leakage: you've (indirectly) fitted to it; the reported number inflates.
Train ≫ val accuracy? The model memorized (overfit). Both low? It underfits.
The test set is evidence about the future; spending it on experiments burns the evidence.
labels: rule: TRAIN teaches · VALIDATION tunes · TEST grades ONCE
press ▶ — the three stacks do three different jobs
train: the model reads only its 12 training rows
validation: you pick learning rate / depth by how it does on the 4 val rows
test: one final grade on the 4 unseen rows — this is the number you report

quiz.q: Your validation accuracy looks disappointing. You check the test set and notice one feature would fix it. What do you do?
options: you may NOT tune on the test — you'd leak it; fix it using train/val, then re-reserve a fresh test set
tune on it — it's just data
delete the test set and use validation as the final grade
report the test number anyway
quiz.why: The moment a choice is made because of the test set, the test set has been 'seen' and its number is no longer an unbiased estimate. The discipline is absolute: test = final exam, once.

title: Linear regression — click to build, and the line chases least error
real_life: laying a straight ruler along a scatter of coins so the 'weight' above and below balances. Least squares is the mathematical version of 'the most balanced ruler' — big deviations hurt extra, so the line avoids them.
intuition: The simplest model: a straight line y = m·x + b. It's chosen by minimizing the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) — the total squared distance from every point to the line. Every fancy model later is a generalization of this idea.

what_moves.description: The line below is the least-squares fit through the 8 dots (slope and intercept are solved in closed form). CLICK the plot to add up to 12 points — the line re-fits live, residual dashes show each point's error, and SSE updates on the right.

key_points: SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Squaring makes errors positive, punishes big misses hard, and keeps the math smooth (differentiable).
For a single line there's a formula (normal equations) — but most real models have no formula, hence gradient descent (next step).
Correlation ≠ fit: a line fits the TREND; points can still be far from it (residuals).
Always plot residuals after fitting — if they show a curve, a line was the wrong shape.
labels: y = m·x + b — the least-squares line
click the plot to add a point (max 12) — the line re-fits instantly

quiz.q: Why do we SQUARE the errors in least squares instead of using plain (absolute) distances?
options: squaring punishes large errors heavily and stays smooth/differentiable — which is what optimization needs
absolute values give negative numbers
squaring makes the sum bigger so it's easier to see
it's tradition, no real reason
quiz.why: |error| is kinked (not differentiable at 0), which breaks gradient-based optimization. error² is smooth, always positive, and makes big outliers costly — the line gets pulled away from them. (MAE exists for outlier-robustness, but MSE is the workhorse.)

title: Gradient descent — walk downhill, one baby step at a time
real_life: crossing a valley in dense fog. You can't see the far side, so you feel the slope under your feet and step downhill. Learning rate is your stride: too small — a day of tiny steps; too large — you overshoot the bottom, then overshoot back, forever.
intuition: Most models have no closed-form solution, so the machine iterates: compute the slope of the error at the current point (the gradient), take a step opposite it. Step size = learning rate × slope. That's it — everything else is engineering around this loop.

what_moves.description: The curve is a loss bowl; the ball sits at the current model. Press Play to step. Drag the LEARNING RATE: small = slow crawl, medium = clean descent, large = oscillation and divergence (the ball escapes and gets reset).

key_points: Step: w ← w − lr · ∂loss/∂w. The gradient is 'the slope of the error' — pointing uphill, so we go opposite.
Learning rate is THE hyperparameter: too small = glacially slow, too large = oscillates or diverges.
Near the bottom the slope → 0, so steps shrink automatically — the ball settles.
This same loop trains a line, a tree-ensemble, and a 100-billion-parameter LLM. Same math, bigger scale.
labels: lr < 0.1: crawl · 0.1–0.5: smooth descent · > 0.7: oscillate · > 1.4: diverge (ball resets)
step rule:  w ← w − lr × slope   (lr =

quiz.q: You set learning rate = 0.99 on a narrow loss bowl. The ball…
options: overshoots the minimum on every step and oscillates wider and wider (diverges)
descends faster — great choice
lands exactly at the minimum
gets stuck at the start
quiz.why: A huge stride ignores where the ball currently is: each step lands on the opposite side with more momentum than it started with. The error grows — 'loss: NaN' in a real training log is this happening.

title: SGD, momentum & Adam — downhill with personality
real_life: pushing a shopping cart over cobblestones. Plain push = you stop at every bump. Momentum = you build rolling mass and carry over bumps. Adam = you also automatically shorten your stride on the rough patches.
intuition: Raw gradient descent is brittle: noisy slopes stall it, narrow ravines make it zigzag. Momentum adds inertia (a shopping cart keeps rolling), Adam scales each step by the recent step-history (self-adjusting stride). Race them on the same bumpy curve.

what_moves.description: Three identical noisy loss curves. All three particles start at the same point on the left and use the same raw slope information — only the step rule differs. Watch who settles at the bottom first and who gets trapped bouncing in the noise.

key_points: SGD: w ← w − lr·g. Simple, but noise makes it jitter and stall on plateaus.
Momentum: v ← βv − lr·g; w ← w + v. Inertia cancels consistent noise and accelerates through flat stretches.
Adam: momentum + per-parameter stride scaling — robust to noisy gradients; the default for deep learning.
These are 'first-order' methods — they only use the slope. The math is trivial; the behavior is profound.
labels: same curve, same start, same slope info — only the step rule differs. The star (x = 3) is the minimum.

quiz.q: On a loss surface riddled with small noisy bumps, momentum is especially helpful because…
options: inertia lets the particle carry through individual bumps while the average direction still points downhill
it uses second derivatives
it reduces the learning rate automatically
it removes noise from the data
quiz.why: Each bump's slope points sideways; averaged over a few steps those sideways kicks cancel, but the true downhill direction adds up. The velocity term is exactly that average — so the particle rolls through the noise instead of stopping at every pebble.

title: Overfitting — when the model memorizes the noise
real_life: a student who memorizes last year's exact exam answers: rehearsal is flawless, the real exam (same subject, different questions) is a disaster. The curve below is the model's version of that trade-off.
intuition: More capacity fits the training data better. Past a sweet spot it stops learning the pattern and starts memorizing the noise — training error keeps falling, test error starts rising. The U-curve on the right is the single most important picture in ML.

what_moves.description: The blue dots are the training data (a sine wave + noise); the yellow diamonds are HELD-OUT test points the model never trained on. Drag the POLYNOMIAL DEGREE: 1 underfits (a line can't bend), 2–3 tracks the wave, 7–8 threads the noise — watch it whip through every training dot while the test points are ignored.

key_points: Underfit (bias): model too simple — both errors high.
Overfit (variance): model too flexible — train error → 0, test error rises.
The sweet spot is where VALIDATION error is minimum — that's how you pick complexity in practice.
Regularization (L1/L2) is a dial that nudges the sweet spot toward simpler models.
labels: sweet spot: tracks the wave, ignores noise
overfit: threading the noise — test error climbs
drag the degree — watch the curve thread the train dots while the test diamonds get ignored

quiz.q: As model capacity increases from small to very large, the validation error typically…
options: falls first, reaches a minimum, then rises (the U-curve)
rises steadily
falls forever
stays flat
quiz.why: Small models underfit (high error on both splits). Growing capacity fits the true pattern → error falls. Past the sweet spot the model fits noise → validation error climbs. Production systems pick capacity at the bottom of the U, on the validation set.

title: K-nearest neighbours — classify by the local crowd
real_life: a new restaurant opens on your street. You don't read its menu — you look at the three nearest neighbours (bakery, bakery, ramen shop) and bet on what it serves. K is how many neighbours you trust.
intuition: The simplest model that isn't a line: to label a new point, look at the K closest labelled points and let the majority vote. There is no training phase at all — the model IS the data.

what_moves.description: Two labelled crowds (blue = class A, yellow = class B). The white probe is yours: CLICK anywhere to move it. The K nearest points get connected, their classes are tallied, and the faint background shows the whole decision boundary. Drag K: small = jagged boundary that chases noise, large = smooth but blunt.

key_points: KNN has no training: prediction = find K nearest, majority vote. Simple, interpretable, and a baseline that always works.
K is a hyperparameter: small K → wiggly, noise-sensitive boundary; large K → smooth, but ignores local structure.
Distance metric matters (Euclidean is the default); features must be scaled the same way or big-scale features dominate.
Cost at prediction time grows with the data (a scan over everything) — the reason for tree/ANN indexes at scale.
labels: class by the K nearest neighbours
click to move the probe · drag K — watch the boundary wiggle (small K) or smooth out (large K)

quiz.q: You lower K from 9 to 1. The decision boundary becomes…
options: jagged and hypersensitive to single noisy points
smoother
identical
more vertical
quiz.why: With K=1 each region belongs to its single nearest point — every noisy point carves out a pocket. Large K averages over more neighbours, which blurs the boundary and smooths out the noise. The K choice is the bias/variance trade-off made concrete.

title: Decision trees — a flowchart of yes/no questions
real_life: 20 Questions. A good game picks questions that halve the possibilities ("is it alive?"), not useless ones ("is it teal?"). A decision tree is 20 Questions that a machine has learned, where 'right answer' = pure leaf.
intuition: The model is a flowchart: each internal node asks one question ("amount > 50?"), each branch answers yes or no, each leaf is a prediction. Questions are chosen to purify the split — Gini impurity is the standard yardstick.

what_moves.description: 12 loan applications (amount, age, approved?). The tree grows in three steps. Step 1 splits on amount > 50: the right side is PURE (all approved) → leaf "YES". Step 2 refines the left side with age < 30: one more pure leaf, and one imperfect leaf (2 of 3 approved — the majority wins). Gini 0 = pure; Gini 0.5 = maximally mixed.

key_points: Gini = 2·p·(1−p). A pure node (all one class) has Gini 0; a 50/50 mix has Gini 0.5. Splits maximize the Gini DROP.
Trees are interpretable: every prediction is a chain of human-readable questions — rare in ML.
A single tree overfits (it can grow until every leaf is pure); depth limits and pruning control that.
Trees hate one feature dominating: scale features or they split on the 'biggest' one. They also love thresholds — no distance math.
labels: right: 6 rows, all 'yes' (pure) · left: 6 rows, mixed
left split by age: 3 pure 'no' + 2/3 mixed
row 2 (amt 42, age 35, YES) is MISclassified by this tree — trees accept minority errors
press ▶ — the tree picks the question that purifies the most

quiz.q: A tree leaf contains 8 rows, all class 'approve'. Its Gini impurity is…
options: 0 — the leaf is pure, no more splitting gain to be had
quiz.why: Gini = 2·p·(1−p) with p = 1.0 → 2·1·0 = 0. The whole game of tree growth is picking the question that drops Gini the most at the split; a pure node has nothing left to gain.

title: Logistic regression — squeeze a line into a probability
real_life: a dimmer switch. The raw signal (line) can be any strength, negative or huge; the dimmer (sigmoid) converts it to a percentage of light. 'Is it on?' is just you deciding that 50%+ counts as on.
intuition: Linear regression predicts numbers; classification needs a decision. Logistic regression runs a line's output through the sigmoid, squashing it into 0…1 — a probability — and you choose where to draw the decision threshold.

what_moves.description: Left: the sigmoid and the current threshold. Right: two classes and the decision line at p = threshold. Drag the THRESHOLD: it moves the line, and the trade-off between 'miss a class-1' and 'falsely call class-1' shifts. Note the name: it's REGRESSION (fits a line) whose output is a PROBABILITY.

key_points: p = sigmoid(w·x + b). The sigmoid squashes any real number into (0, 1) — a probability.
The threshold converts probability → decision. Lower it = call more positives (more recall, more false alarms).
Output is calibrated: p = 0.8 means '80% of points like this were class 1 in the training data.'
Coefficients stay interpretable: wᵢ is how much feature i pushes the log-odds up or down.
labels: low t → call MORE positives (more false alarms) · high t → fewer, safer calls

quiz.q: A model outputs p = 0.6 for a customer. The correct interpretation is…
options: the estimated probability this customer is in the positive class is 60% — a decision needs a threshold
the customer is 60% likely to churn, so label churn
the model is 60% confident about the whole dataset
the answer is 'churn' because 0.6 > 0
quiz.why: p is a probability estimate, not a label. Whether 0.6 counts as 'yes' depends on the cost: flagging a loyal customer for a retention offer is cheap (low threshold); a wrong medical diagnosis is not (high threshold). Same model, different thresholds, different behavior.

title: K-means — clustering without any labels
real_life: sorting laundry into K baskets, then sliding each basket to the center of its pile, then re-sorting by 'nearest basket'. Two rounds and the baskets sit exactly where the piles are.
intuition: No labels, no teacher — just points and a number K. K-means alternates two moves: (1) every point joins its nearest centroid, (2) each centroid moves to the middle of its members. Repeat until nothing moves. The groups discover themselves.

what_moves.description: 36 unlabeled points that secretly form 3 blobs. Press Play: the three centroids (stars) start at the corners and iterate — colors show each point's current team, and the stars glide to their team's center. Drag K to 2 or 4 and re-run: the data votes on what K it really is.

key_points: Input: points + K. That's it — no labels, no features to predict. Output: K groups + centroids.
Each iteration strictly lowers the total within-cluster distance, so it always converges — but possibly to a local minimum (restart with random seeds).
K is a decision: the 'elbow' of the within-cluster-distance curve, or the silhouette score, guides the choice.
K-means finds round, equal-size blobs. Elongated or nested clusters need other tools (DBSCAN, GMM).
labels: /40 — 1) assign to nearest star  2) star moves to team center · repeat

quiz.q: Which of these must you choose BEFORE running k-means?
options: K — the number of clusters (the algorithm never decides it for you)
the labels of the points
the color of each cluster
the final centroids
quiz.why: K-means asks 'give me K' and returns K groups; it has no opinion on how many is right. Picking K is the analyst's job — via the elbow method, silhouette scores, or business logic. Everything else (assignments, centroids) is computed.

title: PCA — rotate the axes to where the data actually spreads
real_life: a long, thin coin lying on a table. You don't describe its position with 'distance from the north corner AND from the east corner' — you describe it by HOW FAR ALONG ITS LENGTH it is, plus a little sideways. The length direction is the first principal component.
intuition: Correlated columns carry the same information twice. Principal Component Analysis rotates the axes so the FIRST axis points along the maximum spread (variance). Most real data is 'long and thin' — so one new axis can hold most of the information, and dimensions can be thrown away.

what_moves.description: The cloud below is deliberately elongated at 35°. The arrows are the principal components: PC1 (gold) runs along the spread, PC2 (purple) perpendicular. Switch to 'keep 1 dim' and every point is projected onto PC1 — watch the loss: only ~7% of the information (the thin sideways jitter) is discarded.

key_points: PC1 = direction of MAXIMUM variance; PC2 = max variance left after PC1, always perpendicular.
'Variance captured' tells you what 93% means: the projected data explains 93% of total spread.
Dimensionality reduction = keep the top k components, drop the rest — cheaper storage + faster models + less noise.
PCA needs centered (and scaled) features; it's unsupervised — the labels are not used.
labels: PCA — the data's own coordinate system
two dimensions keep everything — now collapse one
1 dim: each point projects onto PC1 — only the thin sideways jitter (≈7%) is lost

quiz.q: The first principal component (PC1) is defined as the direction that…
options: maximizes the variance of the projected data
minimizes the variance
points at the largest feature value
aligns with the first column of the matrix
quiz.why: PC1 is 'where the data spreads most'. Projecting onto it preserves the most information; the dropped directions hold progressively less variance. 'Keep 95% of variance' just means keep enough components for their variance to sum to 95%.

title: Cross-validation — rotate the exam across k folds
real_life: a football team assessing its form. One friendly match against a weak opponent proves little. Play five friendlies against five different opponents and average the results — same squad, sturdier estimate.
intuition: One train/test split wastes most data for training and gets lucky-or-unlucky by which rows happened to land in the test set. K-fold cross-validation: cut the data into k folds, and take turns letting EACH fold be the exam. Average the k scores — a sturdier estimate that trains on more data every round.

what_moves.description: 40 rows cut into 5 folds (8 rows each). Step through: each turn, ONE fold (gold) holds out as the test set while the other four (blue) train the model. After five rounds every row has been an exam question exactly once, and you hold five scores to average.

key_points: k is usually 5 or 10 — a bias/variance trade-off between the estimate and the compute cost.
Every row is training data k−1 times and test data once — no row is wasted, no row is over-graded.
Use CV on the TRAIN+VAL data; the reserved TEST split still grades the final model once.
'5-fold CV, 81.2% ± 1.4%' is the honest way to report a model's expected accuracy.
labels: each fold gets exactly ONE turn as the exam — every row is tested once, trained on 4 times
is the exam; train on the other four
final: report 81.8% ± ~2%  —  every row has now been an exam question exactly once

quiz.q: Why use 5-fold CV instead of one big train/test split?
options: each row is used for training AND testing (across folds) and the score averages out split luck
it doubles the dataset
the model trains on all data at once
it removes the need for a test set
quiz.why: One split grades on one lucky/unlucky slice; CV grades on five rotating slices and averages — smaller variance in the estimate, and each model trains on 80% instead of ~70% of the data. The reserved test set still exists for the final once-only grade.

title: The confusion matrix — accuracy is not enough
real_life: a smoke detector. A false alarm (FP) is an annoying 3 a.m. 'beep' — you buy a better battery. A missed fire (FN) is a funeral. Which mistake can you afford depends entirely on the COST of being wrong — accuracy erases that distinction.
intuition: On 95% of a 'rare disease' dataset, the model that always says 'healthy' scores 95% and is worthless. The confusion matrix exposes this: it separates the four outcomes — true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives — and from them come precision, recall, and F1.

what_moves.description: A smoke detector on 10 days: some days there's a real fire (F), some not (N); the alarm either sounds (A) or stays silent (–). Step through the 10 outcomes and watch the matrix cells count up. Precision = 'of the alarms, how many were real'; Recall = 'of the real fires, how many we caught'.

key_points: TP = caught it right · FP = false alarm · FN = missed it · TN = correctly quiet.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP): trust in a positive call. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): coverage of the positives.
F1 = harmonic mean of precision & recall — one number when you need to balance both.
Pick the metric from the COST matrix: spam → precision first; disease screening → recall first.
labels: smoke detector — 10 days, revealed one by one
press ▶ — ten days, one outcome per step

quiz.q: Your detector raises 100 alarms in a year; only 5 were real fires. Which metric is in bad shape?
options: precision = 5/100 = 5% — almost every alarm was a false one
recall = 5% — it missed fires
accuracy = 5%
the confusion matrix is broken
quiz.why: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 5/100 = 5%: the alarms can't be trusted. Recall is about the fires that existed (a different denominator). When false alarms cost trust, raise the alarm threshold — you trade recall for precision.

title: ROC & AUC — one curve for every possible threshold
real_life: an airport security gate. Crank it strict: every terrorist is stopped, but so are 3000 innocent travelers (high TPR, high FPR). Crank it loose: travelers pass freely, terrorists slip through. The ROC is the full map of that dial; AUC summarizes it in one number.
intuition: A good classifier emits PROBABILITIES; the threshold is a policy choice. The ROC curve plots TPR (you caught the real ones) against FPR (you falsely accused the innocent) while sweeping the threshold from strict to loose. The area under that curve (AUC) is the model's skill, threshold-free.

what_moves.description: Left: 40 fire scores (gold) and 40 no-fire scores (blue) — they overlap. The threshold line decides who 'alarms'. Right: the ROC curve — the point rides it as you drag the threshold. A perfect model hugs the top-left corner (AUC 1.0); a coin flip draws the diagonal (AUC 0.5).

key_points: TPR = TP/(TP+FN) — you caught the fires. FPR = FP/(FP+TN) — false alarms per innocent.
Sweep the threshold: every threshold is one (FPR, TPR) point; connect them → the ROC curve.
AUC = 'if I pick one random fire and one random no-fire, the model ranks the fire higher.' AUC 0.8 = 80% of the time.
Calibration matters separately: AUC measures RANKING, not whether 0.8 really means 80%.
labels: top-left = ideal: catch all fires, zero false alarms
drag the threshold — left panel: who alarms · right panel: the point slides along the ROC curve

quiz.q: A model's ROC curve is the diagonal line from bottom-left to top-right. Its AUC is…
options: 0.5 — it ranks fires vs no-fires no better than a coin flip
1.0 — perfect
quiz.why: The diagonal is what you get by ranking randomly: for every threshold, the fraction of fires caught equals the fraction of innocents falsely accused. Area under that line = 0.5. Anything worth deploying beats the diagonal by a visible margin.

title: Ensembles — the committee beats the genius
real_life: five judges, each 70% accurate on hard cases, with DIFFERENT blind spots, agree on a verdict more often than any single judge — because the mistakes don't happen on the same cases. That cancellation IS the ensemble trick.
intuition: One strong model is good; a committee of many slightly-wrong models that disagree is better. Random forest = many decision trees on shuffled data, majority vote. Gradient boosting = each new model fixes the previous model's mistakes. The math: if errors are independent, averaging cancels the noise and keeps the signal.

what_moves.description: The target is circular (inner disk = class 1, outer ring = class 0) — no single line separates it well. Left: 15 'weak' lines, each ~60–75% accurate alone. Right: the majority vote of all 15 — watch the jagged individual errors average out into a near-circular boundary. This is the random-forest intuition in its purest form.

key_points: Bagging (random forest): many models on shuffled subsets, independent, average the votes → variance drops.
Boosting: models train SEQUENTIALLY on the previous model's mistakes → bias drops (XGBoost, LightGBM).
Both need DIVERSE members: identical models add no information (they just repeat the same error).
Ensembles are the default winners of table-data competitions — and the workhorse of production ML.
labels: 15 weak lines vs their majority vote
each line is 60–75% accurate alone — and wrong in DIFFERENT places
≥ 8 of 15 lines agree → the jagged errors average into a circle

quiz.q: An ensemble works better than its members mainly because…
options: the members' errors are diverse, so voting averages the noise out while the signal survives
it always uses more data than a single model
voting is mathematically guaranteed to be correct
it removes the need for evaluation
quiz.why: Averaging cancels only errors that don't correlate. Random forest forces diversity (shuffled data/features); boosting forces it (each tree targets the current mistakes). Clone the same model 15 times and the vote is just that model — diversity is the whole trick.

title: Neural networks — stacked weighted sums that can draw curves
real_life: an assembly line. Each station does one dumb thing (cut, bend, weld, paint). None of the stations 'knows' it's making a chair — but the composition does. Each layer is a station; the product that leaves is more than any one station could produce.
intuition: One neuron computes a weighted sum plus a non-linearity (a sigmoid squish). Stack layers of them and the composition can approximate ANY boundary — circles, spirals, faces. The network has no special knowledge of 'circles'; that shape EMERGES from the stacked sums.

what_moves.description: A 2→4→4→1 network. Press Play to run the forward pass: the input (price high = 0.8, rating low = 0.3) flows right, each neuron sums its inputs with its weights and squishes through a sigmoid, and the single output neuron says 'churn probability 0.83'. The hot edges show where the signal is at each step.

key_points: Neuron: z = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b, then a = sigmoid(z). That's the ENTIRE unit — everything else is repetition.
Without the non-linearity, stacking layers collapses to one big linear layer — the squish is what lets layers bend the boundary.
Width = how many different 'feature detectors' per layer; depth = how many refinement passes.
Training = the same gradient descent you saw on the ball, applied to thousands of weights at once.
labels: forward pass — signal flows left → right
press ▶ — input → hidden layer 1 → hidden layer 2 → output
layer 1: 4 neurons each take a weighted sum + sigmoid — 4 new 'views' of the input
layer 2: 4 more refinements — combinations of combinations
output: one number, 0.83 = 'this customer has an 83% churn probability'

quiz.q: If you removed ALL the activation functions from a deep network, it would…
options: collapse mathematically into a single linear layer — no activations, no curve-making power
become faster and still work fine
train more slowly
need more data
quiz.why: A composition of linear maps is linear: W3·(W2·(W1·x)) = (W3W2W1)·x — one matrix. The non-linear squishes between layers are exactly what make the stack express curved, non-linear boundaries. No squish = no depth advantage.

title: Backpropagation — send the blame backwards
real_life: a kitchen line serves a dish that's too salty. The chef doesn't retrain everyone from scratch — blame flows backwards: seasoning station 70%, sauce 30%. Each station adjusts its NEXT portion by its own share. The dish improves course by course.
intuition: Forward pass: predict. Compare with the truth: error. Backward pass: each weight gets a share of the blame — the derivative of the loss with respect to that weight — and nudges against it. This blame-distribution algorithm is backprop, and it is how every modern model learns.

what_moves.description: A tiny 2→2→1 network, one training example (truth = 0, prediction = 0.86). Step through: forward → error → blame flows back along the edges (red, sized by blame) → weights nudge against their blame → re-run: prediction 0.54. Repeat a few thousand times and the error is ~0. The sparkline is that repetition.

key_points: Backprop = the chain rule, automated: ∂loss/∂w for every weight, computed right-to-left in one sweep.
Blame is PROPORTIONAL: a weight on a hot path (large incoming signal) takes more blame than one on a cold one.
The update is identical to gradient descent: w ← w − lr·blame. No new math, just efficient bookkeeping.
Cost: one forward + one backward pass per example — why GPUs (thousands of examples at once) matter.
labels: press ▶ — forward → error → blame → nudge → re-run
backprop: blame flows back — edge 0.8 takes the most (hot path)
re-run the example: 0.54 — the sparkline is this loop, repeated

quiz.q: Backpropagation computes, for every weight in the network…
options: the gradient of the loss with respect to that weight — its exact 'share of the blame'
the total loss
the number of neurons
the learning rate
quiz.why: The loss is one number; the question 'who should change, and how much?' is answered by ∂loss/∂w for each weight. Backprop is an efficient algorithm (the chain rule, right-to-left) for computing ALL of those at once — then gradient descent does the nudging.

title: Convolutions — a small filter, slid over the whole image
real_life: scanning a crowd for faces. You don't study the whole photo at once — your eye slides a 'face template' across it, and positions with a face pop out. The template is the filter; the list of pop-out positions is the feature map.
intuition: A CNN's first layer slides a tiny filter (e.g. 3×3) over every position of the image, computing one number per position: 'how much of this pattern is here?' One filter = one feature detector. The output is a new, smaller 'feature map' image where that pattern glows.

what_moves.description: The image (left) is a dark band above a bright band — one horizontal edge. The filter (center, moving) is an edge detector: −1 on the top row, +1 on the bottom row. Press Play: it slides left-to-right, top-to-bottom, and stamps its response into the feature map (right). Only the rows where dark MEETS bright light up.

key_points: One filter = one pattern; a layer stacks many filters (edges in all directions, textures, colors).
The SAME weights are used at every position — 'weight sharing'. Fewer parameters, and the detector works no matter where the pattern is.
Stacking layers composes features: edges → corners → textures → shapes → objects.
The filter 'sees' only its 3×3 window — locality is why CNNs excel at images.
labels: convolution — a 3×3 edge detector, slid over the image
done — only the rows where dark meets bright are bright: the map now SHOWS the edge as intensity
/100 · response = (bottom row − top row) of the 3×3 window

quiz.q: Why do convolutions use the SAME filter weights at every position of the image?
options: weight sharing: the pattern means the same thing wherever it appears, and it keeps the parameter count tiny
it's faster to store one weight
images are always the same size
it prevents overfitting completely
quiz.why: A horizontal edge at the top of the photo is the same feature as one at the bottom. Sharing one filter across all positions gives translation invariance for free and uses 9 weights instead of 9×100×100. (And no: nothing 'prevents' overfitting completely.)

title: Recurrent networks — the same block, run over time
real_life: reading a novel sentence by sentence. You don't re-read page 1 for each sentence — you carry a running understanding forward. That running understanding is the hidden state h; each sentence folds into it a little.
intuition: Sequences need memory. An RNN runs ONE block repeatedly: at each time step it reads the new token, updates a hidden state h (a running summary of everything so far), and moves on. The loop IS the architecture — one set of weights, shared across every step.

what_moves.description: The sentence '… it was tired' arrives word by word. At each step the block updates the hidden state (the three bars on the right — a 3-dim summary). Watch the moment 'it' arrives: the network must know 'it' = CAT, and 'cat' left the input window 6 steps ago — only the hidden state carries that link forward.

key_points: hₜ = tanh(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁): the new state mixes the new token with the old state. One formula, every step.
The hidden state is the model's working memory — and in a plain RNN it fades (the vanishing gradient problem).
Long-range links ("it" → "cat") are hard: the signal must survive many steps of blending.
Gates (LSTM) and attention (next step) were invented precisely to fix this fading.
labels: one sentence, word by word — the hidden state updates
'it' needs 'cat' — 6 steps back — only h carries it
SAME weights W,U at every step — the loop IS the model
press ▶ — the sentence arrives, one token per step
'it' arrives — the arc shows the long-range link only the hidden state can bridge

quiz.q: In a recurrent network, what carries information from one time step to the next?
options: the hidden state h — a vector updated every step, summarizing everything seen so far
the input x — it persists in the network
a separate memory bank per time step
the output of the first step
quiz.why: At step t the input is ONLY xₜ; everything about the past is compressed into hₜ₋₁. That's powerful (efficient memory) and the source of the weakness — a 100-dim vector can't hold every detail, so far-back links fade. Gates and attention exist to strengthen that carry.

title: Attention — let every word look at every word
real_life: reading 'The cat sat on the mat because it was tired.' You don't replay the sentence backwards — your eye JUMPS straight from 'it' back to 'cat'. Attention is that jump, turned into a computed weight.
intuition: RNNs compress the past into one fading vector; attention deletes the bottleneck. Every token directly LOOKS at every other token and assigns a weight: 'how much should I copy from you?' Long-range links ('it' → 'cat') are now ONE lookup, no matter the distance.

what_moves.description: Eight tokens, one sentence. The matrix shows every token's attention to every other (row = who's looking, column = who's looked at). Click a token: its row highlights, and arcs show where it actually 'looks' — note how 'it' mostly looks at 'cat' and 'tired', not at its immediate neighbours.

key_points: Attention weight = softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d): each token's query against every other token's key, normalized to sum to 1.
'Self'-attention: queries and keys come from the SAME sequence — every token updates itself from the whole context.
Distance no longer costs: 'it'→'cat' is one lookup whether the gap is 6 words or 6000 — this is what made long documents possible.
Multi-head = several attention views in parallel (syntax, coreference, topical…); the transformer = stacked attention + feed-forward layers.
labels: self-attention — click a token to see where it looks
'): attention is normalized — the row sums to 100%
' copies from · the matrix row = the same weights, drawn as cells

quiz.q: The attention weight between two tokens measures…
options: how much the first token should copy from the second when updating its representation
the spelling similarity of the two words
which token came first
the frequency of the words in the corpus
quiz.why: For each token (the query), every other token offers a 'key'; the dot product scores relevance, softmax turns the scores into proportions summing to 1. The token's new representation is a weighted copy of the others by those proportions. That single mechanism — applied at every position, stacked many times — is the transformer.

title: LLMs & RAG — the model is the brain, your data is the notebook
real_life: an open-book exam with a great librarian. The student (the LLM) is smart but has a short-term memory; the librarian (retrieval) finds the exact two paragraphs that matter and slides them over. Answers now come FROM the book — and you can check the citation.
intuition: A large language model predicts the next token from its context window — brilliant, but it knows NOTHING about your company unless you tell it.
