RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) closes the gap: embed your documents, search for the ones relevant to the question, paste the top snippets INTO the prompt, and the model answers grounded in your data.

what_moves.description: Step through the RAG pipeline for the question 'What's the EU refund window?': the question is embedded and matched against document embeddings (similar meaning = nearby dots); the top-2 snippets are stuffed into the prompt window; the model generates an answer that CITES the snippet. Without RAG, the same model would guess from memory — plausible-sounding, possibly wrong.

key_points: An LLM = next-token prediction at enormous scale; it has no memory between chats and no knowledge of your files.
Embeddings put similar MEANINGS near each other in a vector space — search becomes a nearest-neighbour lookup.
RAG = retrieve top-k snippets → append to prompt → generate. The model only sees what retrieval gives it.
Grounding kills most hallucination on factual questions: the answer has a source you can click. Fresh data needs no retraining.

options: the answer is generated from retrieved, real document snippets in the prompt — with a citable source — instead of from the model's memory
the model becomes smaller
the documents are checked by a human first
retraining makes the model honest
quiz.why: Without grounding the model completes the most plausible text — which is not the same as true. RAG puts the actual policy text in the context window, so the generated answer is a (faithful) paraphrase of retrieved evidence, and the citation lets a human verify. Stale facts? title: Big-O — counting steps, not seconds
real_life: two ways to find a name in a phone book. Flip to the right letter, then scan down (log-ish) vs reading every single page (linear). At 100 pages they're both fine. At 1,000,000 pages one takes a minute, the other takes a day. Same task, different growth.
intuition: Before any code, the analyst's question: how does the work grow as the data grows? Big-O names the growth shape: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic. Two programs that tie at n = 1,000 can differ by YEARS at n = 100,000,000.

what_moves.description: Drag N and watch the four lanes. The bar is the operation count on a LOG scale (each screen width = ×1000); the chip is real time assuming a fast machine at 1,000,000,000 ops/sec. n² is the lane that destroys careers.

key_points: Big-O keeps only the dominant term: 3n² + 40n = O(n²). Constants and small terms are noise at scale.
O(log n) = 'halve the search space each step' — binary search, balanced trees.
Rule of thumb: O(n) at 10⁸ ≈ a tenth of a second; O(n²) at 10⁸ ≈ months. Structure choice IS the performance.
Data analysts meet this constantly: nested loops over two big tables are the n² in your pipeline.
labels: same machine (10⁹ ops/s): n² at 10⁸ ≈ 10¹⁶ ops ≈ 116 days · log(10⁸) = 27 ops ≈ instant

quiz.q: A script takes 2 seconds at n = 1,000 and its complexity is O(n²). At n = 10,000 it takes roughly…
options: 200 seconds — n grew ×10, so n² grew ×100
2 seconds — the data is bigger but the machine is the same
0.2 seconds — bigger data amortizes the cost
20 seconds — O(n) scaling
quiz.why: n ×10 → n² ×100 → 2 s × 100 = 200 s. Spotting '×10 data = ×100 time' is the diagnostic signature of a quadratic loop — and the reason you reach for a hash table or a sort before brute force.

title: Arrays — random access is free, insertion is a relay race
real_life: a row of lockers. You can walk straight to locker #300 (address math) — but if the gym inserts a new locker at position 1, lockers 1..300 all get physically moved one slot right.
intuition: An array is one contiguous block of memory. Because every cell is the same size, the machine computes the address of position i in one arithmetic step — that's why reading a[i] is O(1). But everything is glued together: insert at the front and every element must shift.

what_moves.description: Five-element array below. Step 2: read a[3] — one hop, no scan. Step 3: insert 99 at position 0 — watch the relay: 4 elements move. Insertions at the END are cheap (O(1)); at the FRONT they're O(n). That asymmetry shapes how you build pipelines (append-heavy, not prepend-heavy).

key_points: a[i] = base_address + i·cell_size — one computation, O(1) read.
Append at end: O(1) amortized (occasional resize). Insert at 0: O(n) shifts.
Fixed size (in C) vs dynamic (Python list grows for you) — same address math underneath.
If you're inserting at the front in a loop, you've accidentally built O(n²) — switch to a deque or prepend a marker.
labels: one contiguous block — cells of equal size
press ▶ — read is a hop, insert is a relay
contiguous block: the machine knows every address in advance
read a[3]: one arithmetic step — O(1), no scanning
insert at the END? just one write — O(1). Asymmetry to remember.

quiz.q: Why is reading a[i] O(1) but inserting at position 0 O(n)?
options: reads use address arithmetic (no movement); an insert must shift every later element one slot
arrays are sorted so reads are binary searches
the CPU reads slower than it writes
position 0 is protected by the OS
quiz.why: Reading needs no data movement — just pointer math. Inserting before index 0 moves element 0 to 1, 1 to 2, … n−1 to n: n assignments. The structure is optimized for 'read by position', which is exactly what table work is.

title: Stack vs queue — two ways to hold a line
real_life: a plate pile (stack) vs a coffee-shop queue (queue). Drop 3 plates on the pile: the LAST one is the first you grab. 3 people in the coffee line: the FIRST one is the first served. Same 3 items, opposite exit order.
intuition: Both hold items in order; they differ on WHERE you add and remove. Stack: add and remove at the TOP (last in, first out — a pile of plates). Queue: add at the back, remove at the FRONT (first in, first out — a waiting line).

what_moves.description: Both structures receive A, B, C in the same order. Then the stack POPS and the queue DEQUEUES — watch which item leaves. This one flip (LIFO vs FIFO) is behind undo buttons (stack), function calls (stack), printer jobs (queue), and task queues (queue).

key_points: Stack (LIFO): push/pop at top, both O(1). Undo history, browser back, call stack, DFS.
Queue (FIFO): enqueue back, dequeue front, both O(1). Printer jobs, BFS, rate limiters, message systems (Kafka-style).
Peek = look without removing — free on both.
A deque does both ends; Python's collections.deque and JS (push/shift — beware, shift is O(n) on plain arrays).
labels: same three items — opposite exit order
press ▶ — A, B, C enter both structures
both structures are empty — about to receive A, B, C in the same order
A enters: stack top / queue back
B enters: stack top / queue back
C enters: stack top / queue back — both full: [A B C]
POP the stack: C leaves (the newest). DEQUEUE the queue: A leaves (the oldest).
stack keeps [A B], queue keeps [B C] — the flip is total

quiz.q: You build a 'recent files' menu: each open adds a file, and the user wants the MOST RECENT first. The natural structure is…
options: a stack — the last file opened is the first one out
a queue — fairness is the default
a linked list — all structures behave the same here
an array sorted by date
quiz.why: 'Most recent first' is exactly LIFO: push on open, pop on click. A queue would serve the oldest file first — the opposite of the requirement. Choosing stack-vs-queue is choosing which end of the timeline is the 'front'.

title: Linked lists — cells that point to their neighbour
real_life: a treasure hunt. Each note says 'the next clue is at…' — you can't jump straight to clue #40; you walk the chain. But adding a clue? Write ONE new note and glue it into the chain — nobody else moves.
intuition: A linked list stores items in separate boxes scattered in memory; each box holds a POINTER to the next. No contiguous block, no address math — you reach anything by WALKING from the head, one pointer at a time.

what_moves.description: 4-node list below. Walking to node 3 costs 3 pointer hops (O(k)). But inserting a new node after node 1 is TWO pointer rewrites — zero element movement. Arrays buy fast reads and pay for inserts; lists buy fast inserts and pay for reads. They are opposites.

key_points: Each node: [value | next]. The head is the only address you keep.
Read the k-th node: O(k) hops. Arrays did that in O(1).
Insert after a known node: O(1) pointer surgery (two rewires). Arrays did that in O(n).
A doubly-linked list adds a prev pointer — remove any node in O(1) once you have it.
labels: boxes in separate memory — arrows are the glue
and NEW.next → v2 — two assignments, no moves
walk: head → v1 → NEW → v2 → v3 → v4

insert NEW after v1: rewrite v1.next and NEW.next — 2 ops, nothing moves
the trade-off is exact and total: read speed vs insert speed

quiz.q: You hold a reference to node #500 in a linked list of a million nodes. Removing it costs…
options: O(1) pointer rewires (doubly-linked: prev.next = next.next; next.prev = prev)
O(n) — you must walk to the end to confirm
O(log n) — a tree lookup
O(1) only in a singly-linked list, O(n) in a doubly-linked list
quiz.why: With the node in hand (doubly-linked), removal is two pointer assignments — the rest of the list is untouched. The O(n) cost of lists is WALKING to find a node; once you're there, surgery is instant.

title: Hash tables — the O(1) look-up machine
real_life: a hotel with 10,000 guests but only 60 reception desks. A rule ('desk = (room number × 7) mod 60') assigns every guest a desk; each desk holds a short list of names. To find Ana: compute her desk, scan 2 names. You never scan 10,000 guests.
intuition: A hash table maps keys to buckets: bucket = hash(key) % size. The hash function scatters similar-looking keys across the table, so a lookup is: compute the bucket, walk the (short) chain there. Average cost: constant, no matter how many keys exist.

what_moves.description: Six buckets. Step through: Ana hashes to bucket 2, Ben to 1, Cara to 2 — a COLLISION, so Cara hangs on Ana's chain. Lookup of 'Cara': one hash, then check 2 names. Collisions are expected — the table is sized so chains stay short, which is what keeps the average at O(1).

key_points: hash(key) is a deterministic function: same key → same bucket, every time.
Collisions are normal; resolved by chaining (list per bucket) or open addressing.
Load factor = keys/buckets; rehash (resize + re-insert all) keeps it < ~0.7 → O(1) average.
This is the engine under Python dict, JS object, SQL's join optimization, and your 'is this email a duplicate?' check.
labels: keys scatter into buckets by a formula
press ▶ — insert Ana, then Ben & Cara, then find Cara
6 empty buckets — the hash formula decides where each key lands
Ana: hash → bucket 2 — direct placement, no scan
Ben → 1. Cara → 2: COLLISION — she chains onto Ana (expected!)
lookup 'Cara': one hash + two chain checks — O(1) average, 10,000 keys or 2

quiz.q: Two different keys hash to the same bucket. This is…
options: a collision — expected and normal; the chain holds both, lookup walks it
a bug in the hash function
impossible if the table is big enough
only possible with sorted keys
quiz.why: The birthday problem guarantees collisions once keys exceed the bucket count — and even before. They're handled by design: each bucket keeps a short chain, and the table resizes before chains get long. 'Collision' is a feature of the math, not a failure.

title: Binary search trees — sorted structure, log-depth search
real_life: 20 Questions done efficiently. 'Higher or lower?' against a sorted list of numbers: each answer halves the field. 1,000,000 candidates → about 20 questions. That's a balanced tree doing its job.
intuition: A BST stores sorted data in a tree: left child < node < right child. That one rule means every comparison ELIMINATES HALF the remaining candidates — search, insert, delete all run in O(log n) on a balanced tree. Same rule on sorted input = a degenerate line (O(n)).

what_moves.description: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 80 — each new value compares down from the root until it finds its gap. Then the final step searches for 40: 50 → 30 → 40, three hops. The panel on the right shows what happens when you insert already-sorted data: the 'tree' collapses into a line and every operation costs O(n).

key_points: Invariant: left < node < right. Search: at each node, half the candidates are gone.
Balanced tree: depth ≈ log₂(n). 1,000,000 nodes → depth ≈ 20.
Sorted inserts destroy balance → depth n → O(n) everywhere. AVL/red-black trees re-balance automatically.
In-order traversal (left, node, right) outputs the keys in sorted order — free.
labels: left < node < right — each comparison halves the field
press ▶ — insert six values, then search for 40
search 40: 50 →(left)→ 30 →(right)→ 40 ✓ — 3 hops for 6 nodes; log grows

quiz.q: You insert 1, 2, 3, …, 1000 in order into a plain BST. Searching for 1000 costs…
options: 1000 comparisons — the tree degenerated into a linked line
10 comparisons — the tree stays balanced
500 comparisons — half the tree
1 comparison — it's the root
quiz.why: Each new value is bigger than everything so far, so it always lands on the right: root → right → right → … a chain of 1000. That's why production trees (AVL, red-black) rotate themselves, and why B-trees/B+trees index databases.

title: Graphs — BFS rings vs DFS dives
real_life: spreading a rumor. BFS = a drop of ink in water: it reaches everyone one step away, then two steps away — first contact is guaranteed shortest. DFS = a detective following one lead until it dead-ends, then backtracking to the next.
intuition: A graph is nodes + edges — the general shape of 'things connected to things.' Two canonical walks: BFS explores in RINGS (nearest neighbours first — shortest paths, Facebook 'degrees of separation'), DFS dives to a LEAF before backtracking (puzzles, cycle detection, topological order).

what_moves.description: Seven nodes, seven edges. Toggle BFS / DFS and play: BFS lights up level by level (A → {B,C} → {D,E,F} → G); DFS walks A→B→D→G, backtracks, then E, then C→F. Same graph, completely different visit orders — pick the walk for the question you're asking.

key_points: BFS (queue): visits in distance order → finds the SHORTEST unweighted path.
DFS (stack/recursion): goes deep, backtracks → cycle detection, topological sort, 'is it reachable at all?'.
Both visit every node exactly once; both are O(V + E).
Analyst context: ad-click funnels, dependency graphs, fraud rings — all of it is graph walking.
labels: level 2: neighbours of B and C
G already seen — done, all 7 visited
DFS — dive to a leaf, then backtrack

bfsSteps.note: level 2: neighbours of B and C

dfsSteps.n: G already seen — done, all 7 visited

quiz.q: On an unweighted graph, which walk is guaranteed to find the SHORTEST path (fewest edges) from A to G?
options: BFS — it explores by distance, so first contact with G is via the fewest edges
DFS — it dives to targets faster
neither — only Dijkstra works on unweighted graphs
both give the same path
quiz.why: BFS's ring structure means nodes are discovered in non-decreasing distance, so the first time it touches G is provably shortest. DFS might find A 7-edge path while a 2-edge path exists. (Dijkstra is for WEIGHTED edges; on unweighted it degenerates to BFS.)

title: Sorting — bubble the simple, conquer the smart
real_life: tidying 1,000 receipts by value. Bubble = compare each pair of neighbours, swap if wrong, repeat — works, but painfully. Quick = pick a middle receipt, dump smaller ones left and bigger ones right, then tidy each side — the pile halves itself.
intuition: Sorting is the algorithmic workhorse: 90% of 'find the top/bottom/median' questions are one sort away. Bubble sort is O(n²) — simple, and the reason for its infamy. Quicksort is O(n log n) average — partition around a pivot, recurse on the halves. At n = 1,000,000 the difference is minutes vs milliseconds.

what_moves.description: Same 7-element array, two engines. Play BUBBLE: neighbour comparisons and swaps, pass by pass. Play QUICKSORT: pivot selection, partition swaps, recursion. The step counters make the n log n vs n² gap concrete — and explain why every library sort (Timsort in Python, introsort in C++) is a divide-and-conquer hybrid, never bubble.

key_points: Bubble: adjacent compare-swap, n passes — O(n²). Educational only.
Quicksort: pick pivot, partition (smaller left, bigger right), recurse — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst on sorted input with bad pivots.
Python's built-in sort is TIMSORT: mergesort + insertion-sort hybrid, O(n log n) guaranteed, stable.
'Stable' = equal keys keep their original order — it matters when you sort by one column of a table.
labels: bubble sort — compare neighbours, swap, repeat
quicksort — pick a pivot, partition, recurse

quiz.q: Quicksort's average complexity is O(n log n). WHY does the 'log n' appear?
options: each partition halves the sub-problem, and you do O(n) work per level — log₂(n) levels × O(n) = O(n log n)
the pivot is found in log n steps
the array is scanned only once
it's a property of recursion, unrelated to halving
quiz.why: Every level of recursion processes each element once (O(n) comparisons/swaps) and the partitioning depth is ≈ log₂(n) because each half is (on average) half the size. Multiply: n log n. The 'log' is the halving; the 'n' is the per-level work.

title: Searching — linear scan vs binary halving
real_life: finding 'M' in a dictionary. You don't start at page 1 — you open near the middle, see you need earlier letters, and cut the remaining range in half. About log₂(pages) openings, whatever the book size.
intuition: Unsorted data: scan it (O(n)) — no shortcut exists. Sorted data: halve the search range every step (O(log n)). One value, two orders of magnitude apart at scale: 10⁸ items take 10⁸ checks linearly, or 27 checks binary.

what_moves.description: Ten sorted values, target = 82 (near the end — the worst case for a lucky scan). Play LINEAR: check 0, 1, 2, … until 82. Play BINARY: jump to the middle, keep the half that can contain 82, repeat. The window shading shows the alive half of the array.

key_points: Linear search: O(n), works on ANY data (sorted or not).
Binary search: O(log n), REQUIRES sorted order (or a sorted index).
27 binary checks cover 10⁸ items; a linear scan takes 10⁸.
SQL 'WHERE x = 5' on a non-indexed column is a linear scan; on an indexed column it's a B-tree lookup (binary-search family).
labels: mid = 4: a[4] = 25 < 82 → target is in the RIGHT half

bin.note: mid = 4: a[4] = 25 < 82 → target is in the RIGHT half

quiz.q: Binary search on a sorted array of 1,000,000 items needs at most how many checks?
options: 1,000 — one per thousand
100,000 — the square root
1,000,000 — it still scans everything
quiz.why: Each check halves the range: 10⁶ → 5×10⁵ → … after k checks the range is 10⁶/2ᵏ. Reaching 1 needs k ≈ log₂(10⁶) ≈ 20. That single fact is why indexes (B-trees) exist: they turn 'scan the table' into 'walk 20 levels'.

title: Scale — the moment one machine stops being enough
real_life: one checkout lane vs ten. You can't fix a 50-person queue by making the cashier 10× faster — you can't even make her 2× faster. You open more lanes; the queue splits and each lane stays short.
intuition: Every data system hits the same wall: data grows, but one machine's disk, CPU, and memory do not. Two escapes: scale UP (bigger machine — linear money, hard physical ceiling) or scale OUT (many machines sharing the load — the entire field of data engineering).

what_moves.description: Drag the day's data volume. Both panels process the same data: the gauge shows how loaded each machine is (against a 24h daily SLA), the bars show how long the batch takes. Single machine: one bar, one ceiling. Cluster of 3: the work splits, each bar is a third. Watch where red starts.

key_points: Scale out = parallelism: work that is independent per row/file/customer divides across machines almost for free.
Scale up = one bigger box: cost grows linearly (and hardware grows super-linearly), and you hit a physical ceiling: one disk, one RAM, one failure.
HDFS, Spark, Kafka all exist to make scale-out routine: chunk it, spread it, aggregate it.
Your data stops fitting in one machine's RAM/disk sooner than you think — that point, not the query speed, is what forces the cluster.
labels: same daily data, two machines' worth of answers
Both fine at this volume — enjoy it. Drag N up and watch the single machine break the SLA first.
The single machine is past the 24h SLA — the cluster is still fine. That gap IS data engineering.
Both are red now — but the cluster's answer is 'add node 4' (a commodity box), while the single machine's answer is 'a new building of RAM'.

quiz.q: Your nightly batch takes 20h on one machine. Data will double next quarter. The standard data-engineering answer is…
options: scale out — split the work across several machines (HDFS chunks, Spark executors) on commodity hardware
scale up — buy one bigger machine; more cores, but disk/RAM ceilings barely move
run the batch twice, in parallel, on the same machine — it uses one machine's resources anyway
wait for the data to stop growing
quiz.why: The batch is embarrassingly parallel (rows/files are independent), so N machines give ≈N× speed on commodity boxes. Doubling data on the fixed machine = 40h — already past the 24h SLA. Bigger single machines have hard ceilings and a single point of failure.

title: HDFS — big files, chopped into blocks, copied 3×
real_life: a 12-chapter novel. You don't hand the whole book to one person. You give 4 chapters to each of three friends — and each chapter is written in three ink copies. Lose one friend (or one inkwell)? Nobody loses a chapter.
intuition: One 768GB file can't live on one disk, and one dead disk must not lose the data. HDFS's answer: split the file into 128MB blocks, scatter the blocks across many machines, and keep THREE copies of every block on different nodes. A node dying is an event, not an incident.

what_moves.description: Step through: the file is split, a NameNode keeps the MAP (block → which nodes), and each block is replicated to three DataNodes. Then node B dies — its blocks are still served from their two surviving replicas, and the NameNode schedules fresh copies. Nothing is lost, nothing stops.

key_points: NameNode = metadata only: 'block 7 lives on nodes A, B, C'. It never touches the bytes.
DataNodes = the bytes: each block stored on 3 different nodes (in production: 3 different racks).
128MB block size: big enough to make reads efficient, small enough to spread load and survive failures.
Client reads a block from the NEAREST replica — parallel reads from several nodes at once.
labels: one file · one disk · one failure = total loss
press ▶ — split, map, replicate, then kill node B
768 GB on one disk: won't scale, can't survive a failure
split into 6 × 128 MB blocks (the real file: 10,000+ blocks)
NameNode keeps the block→node map; DataNodes hold the bytes
every block lands on 3 different nodes — 18 copies total
node B dies: its 6 blocks are still served from A and C — HDFS re-replicates, nothing lost

quiz.q: A DataNode holding 400 blocks dies at 3am. What happens?
options: reads keep working — the other two replicas are still there, and HDFS schedules new copies of the now single-copied blocks
the jobs fail — that data lived on that disk
the NameNode rebuilds the data from scratch
nothing — HDFS never replicates, it just hopes
quiz.why: Replication factor 3 means every block has two healthy siblings. The NameNode notices the death, sees those 400 blocks are down to 2 copies, and orders new replicas elsewhere. Downtime ≈ the time to notice; data loss ≈ zero. That is the entire deal HDFS makes.

title: MapReduce — split the work, shuffle the keys, reduce the totals
real_life: counting votes in a country. MAP: each precinct tallies its own ballots into (candidate, count) slips. SHUFFLE: all slips for the same candidate are couriered to one room. REDUCE: each room adds its slips. Every room works in parallel; only the couriers are the bottleneck.
intuition: MapReduce is the pattern the whole field was built on: MAP each input row independently (emit key/value pairs), SHUFFLE (sort+group all pairs by key — the expensive, network-heavy heart), REDUCE (aggregate each key's group). Any computation that is 'sum per group' fits this shape.

what_moves.description: Six sales rows. Play the three phases: each row MAPS to a (city, amount) pair; the SHUFFLE groups pairs by city; each REDUCER sums its group. The output is one table: revenue per city. Same pattern, ten million rows and ten thousand reducers — that's the job.

key_points: MAP is embarrassingly parallel — each row is independent, any machine can do it.
SHUFFLE = the network bottleneck: all pairs with the same key must land on the same reducer (partitioned by hash of key).
REDUCE receives ONE key at a time, already sorted — aggregation is trivial.
This exact shape (emit → group-by → aggregate) is what SQL's GROUP BY, Spark's groupBy, and pandas' groupby all do underneath.
labels: input: 6 sales rows → revenue per city
6 raw rows — the whole world's revenue question in miniature
MAP: each row emits (city, amount) — fully parallel, no thinking
SHUFFLE: same-city pairs are grouped — the network-heavy heart
REDUCE: each group is summed — trivial now that the work is done
output: revenue per city. Same pattern at 10⁹ rows with 10⁴ reducers

quiz.q: What does the SHUFFLE phase actually do?
options: sorts and partitions all key/value pairs so every pair with the same key lands on the same reducer
sorts the input rows by timestamp before mapping
filters out rows with null keys
copies the dataset to a backup cluster
quiz.why: Reduce can only sum 'all Lagos amounts' if all Lagos pairs arrive at one place. Shuffle is the step that makes that true: partition by hash(key), sort within partitions, ship. It's the most expensive phase — which is exactly why Spark's in-memory shuffle matters (next step).

title: Spark — a DAG that keeps intermediates in memory
real_life: passing a tray of dishes down an assembly line. MapReduce: each station sets the tray on a cold shelf (disk), the next station walks over, fetches it, warms it up, does its job. Spark: the tray is handed directly, still warm, station to station. Same dishes, far fewer shelf trips.
intuition: MapReduce writes EVERY stage's output to disk before the next stage can start. Spark builds the whole job as a DAG of stages and keeps the shuffle data in RAM between them — so a 4-stage job pays the disk tax once instead of three times. For iterative work (machine learning!), the difference is 10–100×.

what_moves.description: The same 4-stage job (read → filter → join → aggregate) two ways. Top: MapReduce — every arrow passes through a DISK (write + read back). Bottom: Spark — arrows pass through RAM. Then the timing bars: 3 disk round-trips vs none. The last step shows why ML teams live in Spark: 50 passes over the same data.

key_points: A 'stage' = work between shuffles. The shuffle boundary is where data changes machines — and in MapReduce, where it hits disk.
Spark's shuffle is in-memory (with disk spill as overflow) — the stage boundary costs milliseconds, not minutes.
Iterative algorithms (gradient descent, k-means) pass over the same data dozens of times: disk-bound MR re-reads it every pass; Spark keeps it resident.
Spark is not 'better SQL' — it's a different execution model: whole-pipeline DAGs vs per-stage disk checkpoints.
labels: the same 4-stage job, two execution models
MAPREDUCE — every boundary is a disk round-trip
4 stages → 3 writes + 3 reads from HDFS (the 'disk tax')
4 stages → shuffles in RAM (spill to disk only when RAM is full)
MapReduce: 40 s compute + 3 × 30 s disk = 130 s
Spark: 40 s compute + ≈0 s = ~40 s (the 3× comes from the disk tax alone)
iterative ML: 50 passes over the same data (gradient descent)
MapReduce: 50 passes × (read from disk) = 50 × 30 s ≈ 25 min
Spark: load once into RAM, then 50 in-memory passes ≈ 2 min
press ▶ — the disk tax, and why ML lives in Spark
the job: 4 stages chained together — the shape of most real pipelines
MapReduce: each stage's output is written to HDFS; the next stage reads it back
Spark: the same DAG, but shuffle data moves in memory between stages
same 40 s of compute — MapReduce pays 90 s of disk tax on top
iterative work multiplies the tax: 50 passes × disk = 25 min vs ~2 min

quiz.q: Why is Spark often an order of magnitude faster than classic MapReduce on a 5-stage pipeline?
options: Spark keeps the intermediate shuffle data in memory between stages; MapReduce writes each stage's output to disk and re-reads it
Spark's disks are simply faster
Spark uses a smarter SQL optimizer
MapReduce is single-threaded while Spark is multi-threaded
quiz.why: The bottleneck isn't CPU — it's the disk round-trips at every stage boundary. With 4 boundaries × (write + read) at, say, 30s each, you add 2 minutes of pure IO to a 40-second compute job. Spark replaces those round-trips with in-memory hand-offs. On iterative work the gap explodes: 50 passes × 2 disk touches vs one load.

title: Kafka — an append-only log, partitioned by design
real_life: a restaurant's order pads. Each waiter's pad is one partition: orders on a pad are strictly in the order they were written. The chef reads pad 1 fully, then pad 2. Two orders from the same table always land on the same pad — so the appetizer is never cooked after the dessert.
intuition: Kafka's core is not a 'queue' — it's a COMMITTED LOG: messages are appended, never modified, each with an offset. A topic is split into PARTITIONS (independent ordered logs), and messages with the same key always hash to the same partition — which is how you get ordering guarantees at scale.

what_moves.description: Six steps: the log concept, key-based partitioning, appends, consumers with offsets, a burst that creates LAG, and catch-up. Note what never happens: messages are never reordered inside a partition, and a slow consumer's lag is visible as a number — you can watch it grow and shrink.

key_points: Append-only + offsets = replay: any consumer can re-read from any offset within the retention window.
Key-based hashing → same key, same partition → per-partition ordering (global ordering is impossible by design).
Consumer GROUP: each partition is consumed by exactly one member — scale consumers to add throughput, not to re-read data.
Consumer LAG = last offset − consumed offset. It is the #1 alert metric for streaming health.
labels: press ▶ — log, keying, appends, consumers, lag, catch-up
a log: append-only, every message gets an offset — the address you replay from
keying: hash(customer_id) → same customer always lands in the same partition
producers append at the tail; offsets only grow
consumers read by offset; group membership = one consumer per partition
a burst lands: the consumer falls behind — LAG grows (watch part 1)
catch-up: lag → 0. Within the retention window, any consumer can replay any offset

quiz.q: Two messages for the same customer must be processed in order. Which property guarantees it?
options: keyed hashing puts both messages in the same partition, and one partition is consumed by one consumer in strict offset order
Kafka processes every message in the whole topic one at a time, globally
the consumer sorts by timestamp after reading
nothing — ordering is never guaranteed in Kafka
quiz.why: Kafka's ordering guarantee is PER PARTITION: offsets within one partition are strictly ordered, and one consumer reads them one by one. Keying by customer_id funnels that customer's messages into one partition. Global topic ordering would kill throughput — partitioning is the trade that makes Kafka scale.

title: Lake vs warehouse — schema-on-read vs schema-on-write
real_life: a garage vs a library. The garage (lake) holds everything as-is — boxes, bikes, that weird shelf. Cheap to put things in; finding something means digging through boxes. The library (warehouse) requires every item catalogued before it's shelved — more work on intake, but finding any book is one card-catalogue lookup.
intuition: A data LAKE stores files as-is: cheap, flexible, but the schema is only applied when you query (and you pay that cost every query). A data WAREHOUSE validates and structures data AT WRITE time (star schema, types, keys) so queries run on pre-shaped, pre-indexed tables. Modern shops run both: lake for raw flexibility, warehouse for the reporting layer.

what_moves.description: Left: the lake. Files land as-is; a query must parse, apply a schema, and scan every row — every single time. Right: the warehouse. Ingest validates and loads into a star schema (one fact table, satellite dimensions); a query is an index lookup. Same data, opposite costs — and the costs happen on opposite sides of the pipeline.

key_points: Schema-on-read (lake): flexibility + cheap storage; you pay schema work at query time, and mistakes surface late.
Schema-on-write (warehouse): validation at ingest; queries are fast and consistent, but new data shapes need pipeline changes.
Star schema: one wide FACT table (orders, with measure columns) + small DIMENSION tables (customer, product, time) — the shape OLAP engines are built for.
The warehouse is where your dashboards live; the lake is where everything else lives. The pipeline between them is the ETL (later step).
labels: same data, two homes — the cost moves to one side or the other
every query re-pays the parse cost
ingest: validate types + keys (rejections fail HERE)
star shape = the OLAP sweet spot
press ▶ — files arrive, then live in both worlds
three raw files, three different messes — the same question: where do they live?
lake: they land as-is. No validation, no types, pennies per GB
lake query: parse → apply schema → scan everything → 38 s, every time
warehouse: ingest validates and loads a star schema — the pain is up-front
warehouse query: 0.4 s. Lake = flexibility; warehouse = speed + trust

quiz.q: 'Schema-on-read' means…
options: the schema is applied when you query the data (at read time), not when it is stored
you must declare a schema before any file can be read from disk
the warehouse enforces a fixed schema on everything
data without a schema can never be queried
quiz.why: In a lake the file is just bytes on disk — JSON, CSV, Parquet, whatever. The schema is a VIEW you impose at query time: 'treat column 3 as a date, this field as an amount.' That's why lakes are flexible and cheap to write, and why the same query re-pays the parsing cost every run — and why a bad assumption surfaces in the dashboard, not at ingest.

title: The OLAP cube — slice, dice, roll up
real_life: a 3D shelf of jars. One axis: spice. Another: heat level. Another: size. 'Give me all the medium-heat paprika' = SLICE the heat axis. 'The medium-heat paprika in the small jar' = DICE to one jar. 'How much paprika total per heat level?' = ROLL UP the size axis.
intuition: Every business question is a cell in a cube: dimensions (TIME, REGION, PRODUCT…) are the axes, and the MEASURE (sales) is the value in each cell. OLAP operations are just ways of grouping the cube: SLICE (fix one dimension to a value), DICE (fix several — one cell), ROLL UP (coarsen an axis: month → quarter), DRILL DOWN (the reverse).

what_moves.description: Spin the cube: three axes (TIME, REGION, PRODUCT) and the measure (SALES) living in every cell. Step through the operations and watch which faces light up and what SQL each one compiles to — it's always just a GROUP BY / WHERE on the fact table.

key_points: Cell = one combination of dimension values; its value = the measure (SUM, COUNT, AVG…).
SLICE: WHERE time='Q4' — one face. DICE: WHERE time='Q4' AND region='East' — one cell (or a sub-cube).
ROLL UP: GROUP BY quarter instead of month — 12 cells collapse to 4, values pre-aggregated.
Under the hood there is no magic: OLAP is a star schema + materialized aggregations, and the cube is the mental model that makes the SQL obvious.

quiz.q: 'Roll up from month to quarter' means…
options: aggregating 12 monthly cells into 4 quarterly cells (SUM/AVG per quarter) — the grain gets coarser
deleting the monthly detail from the cube
adding a new dimension to the cube
reversing the grain back to day level
quiz.why: Roll-up changes the GRANULARITY: the month axis is replaced by its parent axis (quarter), and each new cell is the aggregation of the cells it contains. Drill-down is the reverse. Neither changes the data — only the lens. That's why cubes make 'show me the same number, one level up' a one-click operation.

title: DAX — the formula stays still, the context moves
real_life: a kitchen scale. The scale (the formula) always does the same thing: 'weigh what's on the plate.' Put the whole basket on it → 900 g. Put only the East basket on it → 400 g. The scale didn't change; the CONTEXT did.
intuition: In DAX (Power BI's formula language) a MEASURE is a formula like SUM(Sales). The formula never changes — what changes is the FILTER CONTEXT: the set of rows the formula is evaluated over. A dashboard filtered to Region=East doesn't run a different formula; it runs the SAME formula over a different slice of the table.

what_moves.description: Six rows, one formula. Step 1: the page filter Region=East lands — the same SUM now sees 400. Step 2: add Product=Laptop — contexts INTERSECT, the result narrows to 150. Step 3: the same formula on three cards — three contexts, three answers, zero formula changes.

key_points: Measure = formula. Filter context = the rows it runs over. Result = f(formula, context).
Contexts intersect (AND): page filter + card filter + slicer all stack on the same table.
CALCULATE() is the tool that deliberately CHANGES the context inside a measure (add/remove filters).
This is why one Power BI measure serves a KPI on the exec page AND a cell in the detail table — the page decides the context.
labels: press ▶ — the filter lands, the number moves, the formula doesn't
six rows, one measure: Total Sales = SUM(Sales) → 900
page filter Region=East: the context shrinks to 2 rows → 400
three cards, three contexts — the formula is still the same SUM

quiz.q: TotalSales = SUM(Sales) shows 900 on an unfiltered page and 400 on the East dashboard. What changed?
options: the filter context — the same formula re-evaluated over only the East rows
the formula itself — the dashboard must use a different measure
the underlying data changed
DAX caches the first result and divides it
quiz.why: Measures are pure functions of (formula × context). The dashboard's region filter shrank the context from all 6 rows to the 2 East rows; SUM over those is 400. No second formula, no data change. Mastering this one idea is 80% of DAX: when a number 'is wrong', the first question is always 'which context am I in?'.

title: ETL — extract, transform, load (and survive the re-run)
real_life: a mailroom. EXTRACT: pull today's envelopes from three post boxes. TRANSFORM: sort, tear out junk, fix crooked stamps, return duplicates. LOAD: file everything into the right cabinet folder — filed by letter ID, so delivering the same day twice just re-files the same letters instead of duplicating them.
intuition: ETL is the daily plumbing: EXTRACT raw rows from sources (CRM, web logs, invoices), TRANSFORM them into one clean shape (fill nulls, parse currencies, drop duplicates), LOAD them into the warehouse. The unglamorous requirement that separates junior from senior pipelines: a re-run must be IDEMPOTENT — running the same day twice must not double the data.

what_moves.description: Six raw rows from three sources — two are dirty (a null amount, a string currency), one is a duplicate. Play the stages: extract lands everything in staging; transform fixes what's fixable and drops the dup; load lands 5 clean rows. Step 5: the whole thing re-runs — watch the target count stay at 5.

key_points: Transform is where trust is BUILT: type coercion, null policy, dedupe keys, validation rules.
'Dirty data' is not an edge case — it's the normal state of source systems.
Idempotency: load by primary key (upsert) or truncate-and-reload the partition → re-runs are safe.
A pipeline you can't re-run is a pipeline you can't trust — and you WILL need to re-run it.

quiz.q: A nightly ETL fails halfway through LOAD and you re-run it. What prevents double-inserting the first half's rows?
options: idempotent loading — upsert by primary key (or truncate+reload the day's partition), so the re-run lands in the same state

title: Data quality — trust is a measured thing
real_life: airport baggage screening. Every bag passes X-ray (nulls), a scale (range: not 400 kg), and a manifest check (duplicates, freshness: is this bag for THIS flight?). A bag that fails doesn't board quietly — it's pulled, flagged, and a human is told. That's a quality gate.
intuition: A dashboard is only as true as the data behind it. Quality gates make trust explicit: every batch is checked against SLAs (null rate, duplicates, value ranges, freshness) BEFORE it reaches the reporting layer. A gate that fails blocks the load and raises an alert — a dashboard showing a number that failed its checks is a lie with a nice color scheme.

what_moves.description: A batch of 100 rows flows through four checkers into the gate. Step 1: 3 nulls appear (3% > 1% SLA) → gate goes red, dashboard stays on the last TRUSTED number. Steps 2–4: duplicates, a negative price, stale data — each alone is enough to block. The point isn't perfection; it's that bad data can't reach a human decision silently.

key_points: SLAs are numbers: nulls < 1%, dupes = 0, prices > 0, freshness < 24h. 'Looks fine' is not a check.
Gate = hard rule: fail → block the load + alert. The dashboard keeps the last known-good number (labeled as such).
Null rate, dup rate, range, and freshness catch most real-world breakage; add referential checks (FKs) as you grow.
Monitoring quality AFTER load (post-hoc dashboards) is fine for triage — but the gate is what protects the morning meeting.

This reflex is the difference between 'caught it in 10 minutes' and 'explained a 300% lie to the CEO'.

title: Pick the chart by the question, not by taste
real_life: the kitchen drawer. A spoon for soup, a knife for bread, a peeler for apples. None of them is 'wrong' — but eating soup with a knife doesn't fail, it just makes a mess of the answer.
intuition: Chart choice is a mapping: each question type has a visual channel that answers it fastest. Compare magnitudes → lengths (bars). Change over time → positions along a line. Parts of a whole → angles/areas (carefully). Distribution → a histogram. Relationship between two numbers → positions in 2D (scatter). Picking the wrong tool doesn't crash — it just makes the answer harder to see.

Stacked bars = comparison AND composition at once — but non-first segments are read against a moving baseline.

title: What the eye actually compares (channel ranking)
real_life: reading a thermometer (a length — you can say 37.2) vs estimating how much soup is left in a pot (a volume from an angle — 'half? more than half?'). Same kind of question, wildly different precision.
intuition: Not every visual encoding is equal. Position and length are read with ±1% accuracy. Angles: only to ~±15°. Areas: ~±30%. 3D volumes: untrustworthy — perspective, occlusion and the ellipse 'lid' all lie. This is why a bar chart beats a pie chart: it uses the eye's best channel, not its worst.

what_moves.description: Slide the difference between two quantities (2% to 40%) and watch the same question — 'which is bigger?' — answered by four encodings. The bars stay readable the whole way; the pies need ~10%; the squares need ~20%; the cylinders never fully earn your trust.

key_points: Channel ranking: position/length ≫ angle > area > volume > color for MAGNITUDE. Color is excellent for CATEGORIES (hue = identity, not size).
Pies encode magnitude as ANGLE — the second-worst 2D channel — and 6+ slices makes each angle smaller still.
3D charts add a third axis that carries no data but corrupts the two that do (decoration with side effects).
The fix is almost always boring: if the eye struggles, replace the encoding — don't add labels (labels are the eye crying for help).

quiz.why: Psychophysical studies put length comparison error around 1%, angles around 15%, areas around 30%, and 3D volumes in the 'coin flip' zone. That's the entire case for the bar chart: it hands the reader the question in the eye's strongest sense.

title: Charts that lie — the five tricks (and how to spot them)
real_life: a forced-perspective photo. Every pixel is real — nothing is photoshopped — but the person in the back is not actually the size of a car. 'Accurate pixels' ≠ 'true story'.
intuition: A chart can be 100% 'accurate' (every point real, every axis labeled) and still send the reader to a wrong decision. The five classics: (1) truncated y-axis — hide the zero and a 7% change looks like a takeoff; (2) dual axis — two unrelated series on two hidden scales 'correlate'; (3) 3D distortion — volume and perspective inflate the big bars; (4) cherry-picked x-range — show only the months that suit the story; (5) stacked transfer — one series grows inside the stack while the base quietly shrinks.

what_moves.description: The same 8 months of revenue (up 7%, honestly) under five different lies. Step through and read the panel on the right: what the chart CLAIMS vs what is actually TRUE. Your job as the analyst is to be the person who notices the y-axis before the CEO does.

key_points: Truncated y-axis: a line chart with a hidden zero turns a 7% rise into a 'cliff'. Rule: zero-based for magnitudes; truncation only for small changes, clearly labeled.
Dual axis: two series on two independent scales — any two lines can be made to look correlated. Rule: one scale, or don't.
3D: adds a data-free dimension that inflates tall bars and buries the axis. Rule: it's decoration, not information.
Cherry-picked x-range: 'stalled' on M2–M5, 'exploding' on M6–M8. The axis is part of the claim.
Stacked transfer: total looks up while the mix shifts (promos grow, organic base shrinks 10%). Rule: check the BASE series, not just the top line.

title: Color systems — categorical, sequential, diverging
real_life: traffic lights. Diverging by design: red and green meet at the neutral 'caution' amber — the midpoint is meaningful (the stop line). Now imagine the lights were 7 random rainbow colors: every pixel equally 'honest', zero structure. That's a quantity painted with a categorical palette.
intuition: Color has exactly three jobs, and mixing them up is the most common 'technical' lie in business charts. CATEGORICAL: distinct hues for distinct things (order means nothing — hue = identity). SEQUENTIAL: light→dark of ONE hue family for ordered magnitude (light = small, dark = big). DIVERGING: two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint around a MEANINGFUL center (zero, average, target). A map of 'deviation from target' painted in a random rainbow is not colorful — it's wrong.

what_moves.description: Pick a system, slide the number of steps, and watch three rows: (top) the palette, (middle) a data strip using it, (bottom) what a common color-blindness (deuteranopia) actually sees. Sequential and diverging survive the color-blind row — categorical only survives while it stays small (≤5 hues).

key_points: Categorical: distinctness > order. Keep ≤5 hues; beyond that the eye can't keep the mapping, and red–green pairs vanish for ~8% of men.
Sequential: one hue family, light→dark. Magnitude maps, choropleths, heat strips. Never start at full-dark (the light end anchors 'small').
Diverging: two opposite hues, shared neutral center. The center MUST be meaningful (0, mean, target) — diverging around an arbitrary midpoint is a lie with a rainbow.
Test before you ship: run the chart through a color-blindness simulator (the bottom row here) and ask one person with CVD to read it in 10 seconds.

title: Dashboard layout — the 30-second rule
real_life: the car dashboard. Speed, fuel, warnings — the 3 things you need in the next 3 seconds — sit at the top of your sight line. The GPS map (context) is mid-level. The radio EQ settings (detail) are buried in a menu. Nobody reads the EQ before checking the speed.
intuition: An executive gives a dashboard about 30 seconds. The eye scans in an F-pattern: top row first, left to right. So the layout encodes importance: HEADLINE KPIs on top (the answer), TREND/CONTEXT in the middle (the story), DETAIL at the bottom (the evidence, for the curious). One dashboard, one audience, one question. Six KPIs that don't answer one question is not a dashboard — it's a wall of numbers.

what_moves.description: Six cards start in the WRONG rows. Click any card to move it to the next row (headline → trend → detail → headline…). Reach the 6/6 score: every card in the row that matches its job. Watch the '30-second score' and the hints as you go.

key_points: Top row = the ANSWER (1–3 KPIs tied to the dashboard's one question). If you can't name the question, the dashboard doesn't exist yet.
Middle row = the TREND behind the KPIs (sparklines, funnels). Bottom row = the DETAIL tables for the curious — never in the headline row.
One dashboard ≠ one department's everything. Split by audience: the exec page, the ops page, the debug page.
Density check: if a reader can't say what's 'on fire' in 30 seconds, you have a data dump, not a dashboard.

quiz.why: The exec row answers 'are we OK?' with one number each; a 40-row table answers 'where exactly?', which only some readers need, and only after the headline. Detail belongs at the bottom or behind a click — leading with it guarantees nobody sees the KPIs.

title: Data storytelling — context first, callouts last
real_life: a photo of a flooded road. Alone: 'a road with water'. Add a sign: 'detour ahead'. Add an arrow and a time: 'go this way, 10 minutes'. The water never changed — the STORY was built around it.
intuition: The same chart tells three different stories depending on what surrounds it. Version 1: a naked line — the reader sees 'a line… so what?'. Version 2: add CONTEXT (last year, the plan) — now the reader sees 'we missed plan in September'. Version 3: add the CALLOUT ('summer promo ended') and the ACTION ('re-run the promo Oct–Nov') — now the chart ends in a decision. A chart without a next step is decoration; a story without context is a guess.

what_moves.description: One revenue line (the September dip is real in all four versions). Step through and watch the reader's state on the right move from 'huh?' to 'do it'. The chart never changes except for what's ADDED around it — that's the whole craft.

key_points: Order of the story: CONTEXT (what should we be seeing?) → FINDING (what are we actually seeing?) → CAUSE (why?) → ACTION (what do we do, and what changes when we do?).
Benchmarks do the work: a line against last year and against plan is a different animal from a line alone.
Callouts are sentences, not arrows: 'Sep: promo ended → revenue −18% vs plan' beats a red circle.
Every story needs a next step with a number: 're-run promo, $18k, back to plan by Dec' — otherwise the meeting ends and nothing happens.

title: The analyst loop — question → data → insight → action

real_life: a doctor. Symptoms (question) → tests (data) → diagnosis (insight) → treatment (action) → follow-up visit (new data). If the follow-up is worse, the diagnosis changes. A doctor who never re-checks the patient isn't practicing medicine — they're selling reports.
intuition: Real analysis is not a line, it's a LOOP. A business question earns a data pull; the data earns an analysis; the analysis earns an insight; the insight earns an ACTION; and the action changes behavior, which creates NEW data, which raises the NEXT question. Analysts who work in a straight line ('crunch → report → done') stop creating value at the report. The loop is what makes the job repeatable.

The feedback beat is the promotion: 'we shipped the fix, here's what the new data says' turns a report into an operating system for the business.
If your work ends at 'here's the PDF', you did 4/5 of the job — the 5th beat is why they keep calling you.

title: Notebook to production — the three gaps
phase_title: Ship it — from notebook to career
real_life: a home-cooked meal vs a restaurant kitchen. The recipe works in YOUR kitchen. Scaling to 50 covers a night needs: a prep schedule (someone who isn't the chef still feeds the diner), a way to spot a bad dish BEFORE the customer eats it, and plating where the guest actually is. The recipe alone gets you a dinner party, not a restaurant.
intuition: A notebook that runs on your laptop is not a product. Three gaps stand between it and the real job: (1) it must RUN WITHOUT YOU — a schedule, idempotent loads, no human clicks (phase 6's ETL rules); (2) it must FAIL LOUDLY — alerts on null spikes, freshness, breakage, plus auto-retry, so a dead pipeline is discovered in minutes, not at the Monday meeting; (3) it must be CONSUMED — a dashboard or an API where decisions actually happen, not a PDF in a chat channel. Close the gaps in that order and the notebook becomes infrastructure.

what_moves.description: Step through the three gaps. At each stage the readout names 'what breaks without this' — because the gap only exists until the thing breaks once, and it WILL break once.

key_points: Gap 1 · Run without you: a scheduler (cron) + idempotent loads (phase 6) + a versioned repo. 'Works on my machine' is the first gap, and the one that costs the most sleep.
Gap 2 · Fail loudly: quality gates + alerts (phase 6) + auto-retry. A silent dead pipeline is worse than no pipeline — people act on stale numbers.
Gap 3 · Consumed where decisions happen: dashboard (phase 7) or API. A PDF in Slack is read by zero decision-makers; a KPI on the exec page is read by all of them.
The order matters: schedule before alerts, alerts before distribution. Distribute a fragile pipeline and you're shipping bugs to the whole company on a timer.

title: The 30-second insight — the pyramid (execs read top-down)
phase_title: Ship it — from notebook to career
real_life: the doctor calling your family after surgery. First sentence: 'the surgery went well, she'll be home Friday.' Only THEN the procedure details, the test results, the aftercare. Lead with the evidence ('so the surgery was a 6-hour procedure, and the labs showed…') and you've just raised their blood pressure for nothing.
intuition: Executives process top-down: the recommendation first, then the two or three supporting points, then (if they still care) the evidence. Presenting bottom-up — 'let me walk you through the data' — spends their patience on the evidence before they know what you're asking for. The Pyramid is the shape: RECOMMENDATION at the top (one line), SUPPORTING POINTS below it (2–3), EVIDENCE at the base (the appendix that proves it, for whoever asks). The order you SAY things is the pyramid; the order you BUILT them doesn't matter.

what_moves.description: Four blocks are on the table in random order. Click them in the order you would SAY them in the meeting. The pyramid builds in speaking order, and the exec's patience meter scores you: the recommendation at the top is worth the most; every block that lands out of place spends patience.

key_points: Top line = the RECOMMENDATION with the number: 'double the EU budget — revenue +$40k/wk'. One line, a decision, a stake.
Supporting points: 2–3, each one sentence ('it's all EU-driven', 'payback in 5 months', 'risk is capped at $18k'). No data dumps at this level.
Evidence lives at the BASE and in the APPENDIX: shown only if asked. 'Here's the 40-row table' is a level-3 response, not a level-1 one.
The email mirrors the pyramid: subject line = recommendation, line 1 = the number, body = the 2–3 points, attachment = the evidence.

title: The interview loop — technical, case, take-home
phase_title: Ship it — from notebook to career
real_life: a driving test. The examiner isn't scoring your destination — they're scoring the PROCESS: mirrors, signaling, checking the blind spot before the turn. A fast arrival with no mirrors fails the test. Interviews the same: the answer is 40%, the visible process is 60%.
intuition: Data interviews run three rounds, each testing a different muscle: (1) TECHNICAL — SQL on a whiteboard (window functions, joins, aggregates) plus pandas and stats intuition; (2) CASE — an unstructured business question ('how would you measure success of a new onboarding flow?') where framing beats fluency: goal → north-star metric + guardrails → hypotheses → data plan, in that order, before any 'data' is touched; (3) TAKE-HOME — a small project judged on depth AND communication: they often grade the one-page summary more heavily than the notebook. The common failure in all three is the same: performing at the level of the question asked, instead of the level of the decision implied.

what_moves.description: Step through the three rounds. Each panel gives the round's format and the single highest-leverage move in it. The quiz at the end is the case round's first move — the one interviewees most often skip.

key_points: Technical: confirm edge cases OUT LOUD before coding (duplicates, nulls, ties in ranking, empty tables). Examiners award points for the questions, not just the query.
Case: the first 5 minutes are framing, zero data: 'the decision is X; the north star is Y; guardrails are Z; my first hypothesis is W; here's the data I'd pull, in this order.'
Take-home: the one-page summary IS the interview — write it for a non-technical reader using the pyramid (previous step). Code they can't read is fine; a summary they can't follow is fatal.
Across all rounds: think out loud. A wrong answer with a visible, recoverable process beats a right answer that appears by magic.

title: Your capstone — the brief (and the stranger test)
phase_title: Ship it — from notebook to career
real_life: the first solo flight. The instructor still sits in the back — but the checklist is YOURS: pre-flight (question), taxi (data), takeoff (analysis), the turn (insight), landing (action + docs). You don't get credit for the instructor's skills; you get credit for the checklist you can run alone.
intuition: The last step of the course is yours. You get a brief, a dataset, and a decision — and you run the whole course against it: the question earns the data (p1), the data earns the analysis (p2, p3), the analysis earns the insight (p4 where a model is honest), the insight earns the story (p7), and the story earns the ship (p8: A/B, docs, the pyramid email). The success criterion is the STRANGER TEST: a person who knows nothing about the project can state the question, your one insight, and the decision — in 10 minutes, unaided. Pass that and you have the first real artifact of a data career.

what_moves.description: Pick one of the three ShopFlow briefs. The roadmap shows which phase of this course each stage draws on, and the stranger-test checklist is the definition of done. There is no 'correct' brief — there is only one you'd defend in front of a hiring manager.

key_points: A brief is worth its decision: all three below have money, a deadline, and a stakeholder who has to DO something with the answer.
The roadmap is the course in miniature: SQL (p1) → stats/EDA (p2, p3) → a model only where it's honest (p4) → story + dashboard (p7) → A/B + pyramid communication (p8).
Scope is the skill: a capstone that answers ONE decision well beats three that each answer a lot. Cut until a stranger can hold the whole thing in 10 minutes.
The stranger test is a rehearsal for every stakeholder you'll ever meet: if a stranger can't state question → insight → decision, a CFO can't either — with more patience spent.
